title: MacWhisper update brings real-time meeting transcripts, improved speaker recognition, more
snippet: My transcription tool of choice on the Mac, MacWhisper, got another major update today with real-time meeting transcripts, significantly improved speaker recognition, tighter integration with Apple Intelligence, and a new transcription model. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
My transcription tool of choice on the Mac, MacWhisper, got another major update today with real-time meeting transcripts, significantly improved speaker recognition, tighter integration with Apple Intelligence, and a new transcription model. Here are the details.

MacWhisper gets deeper Apple Intelligence integration

I’ve written in the past about how much I rely on MacWhisper, particularly as part of my podcast production workflow.

MacWhisper was one of the first AI-powered transcription tools for the Mac. Since indie developer Jordi Bruin launched it in 2023, it has been on a relentless streak of improvements and expanded support for new models, services, and workflows.

That has included everything from automatic meeting recording and speaker recognition to watched folders, system-wide dictation, local and cloud AI models, and integrations with services such as Notion, Zapier, Obsidian, and n8n.

Today, MacWhisper was updated to version 15.2, introducing an improved speaker recognition powered by NVIDIA’s Nemotron 3 Diarization model, which was announced just hours ago.

It supports up to 8 speakers and can also be used during live meetings in the new realtime meeting view!

Which brings us to another major addition in today’s update: real-time meeting transcriptions.

This feature had been sitting near the top of MacWhisper’s public roadmap for a while, and it is now here, allowing users to follow, refer back to, copy, or transfer a live transcript as the meeting unfolds.

You can keep the window above your other apps to follow along, and your recording and transcript are saved when the meeting ends.

When it comes to the actual transcription models, MacWhisper 15.2 adds Alibaba’s QWEN3-ASR transcription model with support for 22 languages, in addition to a tighter integration with Apple Intelligence, Siri, Spotlight, and Shortcuts on macOS 27.

Now, users running macOS (including in the EU) can search for transcripts system-wide, open them with Siri, pull their text into Shortcuts, and refer to the transcript currently on screen in Siri or Apple Intelligence requests.

Finally, MacWhisper 15.2 adds folders and subfolders for organizing transcripts and meetings, with support for dragging existing transcriptions into them from the sidebar.

title: iOS 27.2: New features, release date, more
snippet: Apple has kicked off beta testing of iOS 27.2, and the update brings several notable changes and new features. Here’s everything you need to know about iOS 27.2, which will likely be released to iPhone users as soon as next month. more…
fullText:
Apple has kicked off beta testing of iOS 27.2, and the update brings several notable changes and new features. Here’s everything you need to know about iOS 27.2, which will likely be released to iPhone users as soon as next month.

Why iOS 27.2 and not iOS 27.1?

Apple released iOS 27 on September 14, bringing a ton of new iPhone features, including Siri AI. iOS 27.2 entered beta testing just two days later on September 16.

What happened to iOS 27.1?

Apple previously confirmed that iPhone Duo will ship with iOS 27.1 when it’s released on October 23. This means iOS 27.1 includes many references to the iPhone Duo in its code, which Apple wants to keep under wraps until the device ships. iOS 27.1 will therefore be exclusive to the iPhone Duo.

The software paths for iPhone Duo and other iPhone models will then converge, either with an iOS 27.2.x software update or perhaps with iOS 27.3.

So, things will be awkward for a little bit, but everything will eventually return to normal.

iOS 27.2 new features

Redesigned Health app

At the iPhone 18 Pro event, Apple showcased an all-new version of the Health app that it said would be coming later this year. That new app has entered beta testing as part of iOS 27.2.

The redesigned Health app is split into three tabs: Insights, Longevity, and Browse. The app features an all-new design that dynamically adapts based on your data, including Apple Intelligence. The Longevity tab includes a new Health age feature that uses Apple Watch data to show how your metrics track relative to your actual age.

The new Health app likely won’t be released with iOS 27.2 next month. Instead, this is Apple kicking off beta testing of the new app before ultimately releasing it to everyone later this year.

Read more: iOS 27.2 introduces Apple Health app overhaul, here’s what’s new

Profiles in the TV app

The Apple TV app in iOS 27.2 adds support for profiles for the first time. This feature has been available on tvOS for several years, but this is the first time it has come to iPhone.

Read more: iOS 27.2 gives Apple TV a new profiles feature on iPhone

More Siri AI languages

Siri AI is the big new feature in iOS 27, and iOS 27.2 expands the feature to even more users. The update adds Siri AI support for the following languages:

French

Japanese

Korean

Portuguese

Spanish

Dual Capture mode for Group FaceTime

In iOS 27, Apple added a new Dual Capture feature for FaceTime that lets you have your front and rear cameras active at the same time. The person on the other end of the call will see you as well as whatever you’re looking at. iOS 27.2 expands this feature to Group FaceTime calls for the first time.

Dual Capture requires an iPhone 17 or later, and everyone on the call needs to be running iOS 27.

Read more: iOS 27.2 makes FaceTime’s best new feature even better

Odds and ends

In Apple Podcasts, the “Up Next” queue has been renamed to “New Episodes.” The “Continue Playing” section is directly below New Episodes. Episode lists also now use color-matched backgrounds based on the podcast art.

In the Music app, some of the red icons and accents have been changed to black.

iOS 27’s Call Context feature, which surfaces information right on your screen when calling a business, has been expanded to include anniversaries.

There are small changes to the alarms interface in the Clock app, such as smaller text for the AM and PM labels.

Hints at more features to come

Finally, iOS 27.2 code hints at a handful of other new features that could come soon to iPhone users. This includes live countdowns for new album releases in Apple Music, third-party app support for Describe a Shortcut, and new themes for CarPlay Ultra. iOS 27.2 also shows Apple is continuing its work on an anti-snatching feature for iPhone.

These features aren’t live in iOS 27.2 just yet, but the code suggests they are in active development inside Apple.

iOS 27.2 release date

iOS 27.2 is expected to be released to iPhone users sometime in October. Apple promised that Siri AI would come to new languages in October, and iOS 27.2 adds those new languages, so the update needs to be released before November for Apple to hit that promise.

Wrap up

Are you running the iOS 27.2 beta? Have you found any useful new features? What do you think of the new Health app? Let us know down in the comments.

title: Report: Apple working on new Vision Pro, with different form factors on the table
snippet: After the release of Vision Pro, everyone wanted to know how long it would be before the company could release a lighter version that isn’t so bulky on your face. For the longest time, we had been looking forward to a so-called Vision Air, codenamed N100. That project was shelved last year, though the company is working on a new project with similar aspirations, per Bloomberg. more…
fullText:
After the release of Vision Pro, everyone wanted to know how long it would be before the company could release a lighter version that isn’t so bulky on your face. For the longest time, we had been looking forward to a so-called Vision Air, codenamed N100. That project was shelved last year, though the company is working on a new project with similar aspirations, per Bloomberg.

Unlike the previous N100 project, it doesn’t seem the new project, N224, is necessarily targeted at being a lower cost offering. It could instead be a successor to the current M5-based Vision Pro model, though it might still come in at a lower price while offering the flagship experience.

This new version seems relatively early in the works, with Bloomberg reporting that it could arrive between late 2028 and early 2029. That said, it isn’t quite clear what exactly Apple will be going for. The company currently has four concepts in the works.

One of the concepts is similar to the recently unveiled Meta VR glasses, which offloads the compute and battery to an external puck. Given the fact that Vision Pro already has an external battery, offloading the compute doesn’t necessarily seem like a major hurdle, though you’d need better thermals and more efficient compute to pull that off.

On the other hand, some Apple executives reportedly don’t love the idea of an external puck, and “want the company to stick with something closer to an all-in-one design.”

Design wise, Apple might get a bit more experimental compared to the current Vision Pro, with the company supposedly considering other material choices. From the Power On newsletter:

One design in testing retains the basic egg-shaped form of the current Vision Pro, but Apple is actively exploring ways to reduce its weight by experimenting with plastic, titanium, other metals and various materials. The company has also continued to explore a standalone puck that combines the computing components and battery, similar to the approach used by Meta’s recent VR Glasses.

Wrap up

Time will tell what Apple will actually end up delivering. Given the A20 Pro chip being incredibly performant at its thermal envelope, it seems highly likely that in another 2 years, we could have an A-series chip capable of running visionOS at a higher capacity than the current M5, while not needing active cooling.

	

I do think Apple should go all in on the Meta VR glasses idea. Even at a higher price point, I think the form factor makes a ton of sense. Apple silicon, EyeSight, and visionOS will allow the product stand out.

What do you think of this new Vision Pro news? Are you a current Vision Pro owner, or are you still skeptical of the idea of headsets? Let us know in the comments.

title: Apple hit with $5.7 billion verdict over Taptic Engine patent infringement
snippet: Apple must pay $5.7 billion for infringing on patents held by Taction Technology, a US jury ruled on Friday. The patents relate to Apple’s Taptic Engine, which is the hardware Apple uses to provide haptic feedback for notifications, button presses, and other interactions. Taction first filed the lawsuit in 2021, alleging Apple had “infringed and continues to infringe, directly and indirectly” its patents. more…
fullText:
Apple must pay $5.7 billion for infringing on patents held by Taction Technology, a US jury ruled on Friday. The patents relate to Apple’s Taptic Engine, which is the hardware Apple uses to provide haptic feedback for notifications, button presses, and other interactions.

Taction first filed the lawsuit in 2021, alleging Apple had “infringed and continues to infringe, directly and indirectly” its patents.

As reported by CNBC, the lawsuit centered around two patents:

U.S. Patent No. 10,659,885

U.S. Patent No. 10,820,117

Both patents are focused on a “vibration module for applying vibrational tractions to a wearer’s skin.” Taction argued that Apple’s Taptic Engine infringes upon its patents, saying that Apple was “capitalizing on Taction’s innovation and success.”

Apple’s Taptic Engine first debuted as part of the Apple Watch in 2014 and came to the iPhone 6s and iPhone 6s Plus the following year, replacing the older vibration motor.

In a statement, an Apple spokesperson said:

“While we thank the jury for their consideration, we strongly disagree with today’s verdict and the damages awarded, which are entirely unsupported by the facts.

Apple’s Taptic Engine is fundamentally different from Taction’s technology, which Taction’s own testing of Apple’s products confirmed during trial. Apple does not use Taction’s technology, and we will appeal.”

Taction Technology is a California-based company that describes itself as being “obsessed by sound.” The company says that its “Transporter Technology powers the game-changing Corsair HS60 Haptic headphones, and will soon be powering other premium headphones from major manufacturers.”

In a statement to CNBC, Taction’s lead counsel said:

“We’re happy the jury found for Taction and vindicated its patent rights. Taction waited five and a half years for this case to get to trial, so it was a long time coming.”

You can read the original complaint for patent infringement filed by Taction here and Friday’s jury ruling here.

title: What do you actually use a laptop for, and would Googlebook be able to do it? [Poll]
snippet: Following a mediocre teaser back in May, Googlebook is officially here and, well, I’m still pretty skeptical. I’m not sure I see Google’s vision of this new lineup or laptops because, frankly, I’m not solving any of the problems Chromebooks already faced. more…
fullText:
Following a mediocre teaser back in May, Googlebook is officially here and, well, I’m still pretty skeptical. I’m not sure I see Google’s vision of this new lineup or laptops because, frankly, I’m not solving any of the problems Chromebooks already faced.

Our initial coverage of Googlebook is live, with Abner, Jordan, and Damien all walking away with a good first impression of Google’s efforts.

Google fully details Googlebooks: $899+, October launch, & more

Googlebook OS hands-on: It’s Android, stupid

Googlebook hands-on: What makes a laptop, a laptop? [Video]

Yet, I’m unconvinced thus far. I’ve yet to get my hands on a Googlebook and, as someone sitting mostly in the same boat as you, our readers, I’m yet to be sold on this new platform. I simply don’t understand why it exists, even more so why Google seems to think it will succeed.

Google’s entire pitch around why you should buy a Googlebook more or less boils down to smartphone integration – specifically Android integration. Googlebook takes existing tools from ChromeOS and supercharges them, giving you the ability to mirror apps, sync files, and do a whole lot more between your Android phone and your laptop. And it does sound pretty good! As someone who currently juggles a MacBook with various Android phones, there are integrations I wish existed; instant hotspot and proper Quick Share support (AirDrop works, but tends to be wildly slow) are at the top of that list. 

	

Googlebook is delivering the MacBook + iPhone experience, just for Android users. That’s the pitch.

Where it falls flat for me is in the apparent functionality. At its core, Googlebook is Android, just with a desktop experience built on top. The core stuff is there – desktop-class Chrome browser, customizable desktop, keyboard shorts, the lot. But the app ecosystem is built around Android apps, web apps, and Linux apps. The same core as ChromeOS, just with a different priority and with better performance on the Android app side, as Abner and Damien both noticed.

That’s where I’m struggling to get on board.

There’s plenty you can do on a Googlebook, sure, just like there was plenty you could do on a Chromebook. But you’re still making a trade-off. Google pointed out that around 70% of things people do on a laptop are done through their browser (Chrome, of course). And, yeah, I’d say that’s about how much I do in the browser on my Windows desktop or my MacBook. That other 30%, though, is the “make or break” that eventually broke me on ChromeOS. For me, it largely came down to Adobe’s apps which, as it stands, still aren’t replicated on Googlebook. On Google’s own website, the company touts a Googlebook’s ability to use Photoshop and Lightroom, but that’s just with the mobile apps – not the full-featured apps you can use on you know, most other laptops. 

Google knows people use these apps; otherwise, it wouldn’t take up a place on this site in the first place – the same goes for games, where Google advertises tons of popular titles like Forza Horizon, Marvel Rivals, Arc Raiders, and more, with only two of the games shown running natively and the rest delivered via GeForce Now.

The market has pretty clearly spoken in this regard. Chromebooks are out. There are remarkably few consumer-focused Chromebooks on the market today and, especially on the high end, it seems like hardly anyone is buying them – Google itself gave up on first-party Chromebooks over five years ago. 

To me at least, the reasoning seems obvious. When Chromebooks hit their stride, the market was full of compromises everywhere. There was no one perfect answer. But that’s changed in recent years. Apple’s M-series chips ushered in a new era for the MacBook which, in turn, influenced some major improvements across Windows laptops. Fast forward to today and there’s no lack of powerful, battery-efficient, thin & light laptop options and, despite “RAMageddon” ruining the price side of things, there’s been a huge push for more affordable machines in the wave of MacBook Neo and its clones – and those are very popular too. Giving up access to a full collection of full-featured apps for a lightweight operating system that gets roughly the same battery life for roughly the same price is a no-brainer, which means that Chromebooks are relegated to a niche. In enterprise/schools, for more affordable machines, for low-end hardware, ChromeOS still makes a lot of sense, but it’s a tough sell basically anywhere else, so you might be able to see why I’m so confused by Googlebook.

Googlebook’s pitch, again, isn’t bad, but does it make sense in today’s market? Who’s buying a laptop that’s inherently (and inarguably) restricted in what it can do, especially at a time when laptops are wildly inflated in price in the first place due to component shortages? 

This is the part where I turn the floor over to you.

Do you think Googlebook has stuck the landing? Has Google’s pitch resonated with you? 

	

Even more so, what are you using a laptop for in the first place? That’s perhaps the most important question around this. As mentioned, I’m personally using my laptop mostly in Chrome, with non-Chrome apps including the likes of Photoshop/Lightroom/Premiere, Spotify, Slack, and a handful of assorted other tools. There are a few of those I can replace – Spotify’s tablet interface should be a treat on a laptop, though I think Slack will be awful given how the Android app lacks any semblance of big-screen optimizations (on Android, as they’re immediately giving Apple something better), so maybe the Linux app will be better.

That’s just me. There are infinite ways people use their laptop. So, looking at what you do today, do you think a Googlebook can do it all? Vote in the poll below, then leave a comment.

title: Microsoft quietly ending ‘Copilot+ PC’ branding for Windows laptops
snippet: After a couple of years of relentlessly pushing it, Microsoft is seemingly ending its Copilot+ PC branding for Windows laptops. more…
fullText:
After a couple of years of relentlessly pushing it, Microsoft is seemingly ending its Copilot+ PC branding for Windows laptops.

Windows Central spoke with executives from Microsoft and Qualcomm about the lack of Copilot+ PC branding on the latest Surface machines. While it’s not been said explicitly, Surface CVP Brett Ostrum all-but-confirmed the end of that branding by saying:

…these are not called Copilot+ PCs. They do meet all the requirements of our previous bar for what Copilot+ devices are. We still lean into the narrative around AI on the edge and being able to have a hybrid solution out there.

	

Copilot+ PC branding was generally used to identify a laptop that met certain hardware requirements around AI features, particularly the NPU, which virtually every mid-high-end laptop already supports. Windows Central further points out that Nvidia’s RTX Spark push has been absent of any mention of Copilot+ PC branding.

Microsoft started using this branding back in 2024, but when the flagship feature of the Copilot+ PC, Recall, was met with backlash, the branding became little more than a hardware checkbox that consumers didn’t fully understand. 

	

The only big question left – does this mean the Copilot Key is going away?

title: AirPods just got a long-requested feature in new software update
snippet: While it was overshadowed by release of iOS 27, Apple also released a new software update for AirPods this month. The update brings a long-requested feature to supported AirPods models: custom EQ. more…
fullText:
While it was overshadowed by release of iOS 27, Apple also released a new software update for AirPods this month. The update brings a long-requested feature to supported AirPods models: custom EQ.

AirPods software details

The latest AirPods firmware build number is 9A350 for AirPods 5 and 9A348 for the other models below. The update is available for the following AirPods models:

AirPods Pro 3

AirPods 4

AirPods 4 with Active Noise Cancellation 

AirPods 5

AirPods 5 with Wireless Charging Case

AirPods Pro 2 (Lightning and USB-C)

AirPods Max 2

Apple says that AirPods firmware updates are automatically installed while your AirPods are charging and within Bluetooth range of your iPhone, iPad, or Mac that’s connected to WiFi. You can check the firmware version of your AirPods in the Settings app on iPhone. 

Custom EQ comes to AirPods

Once you install the AirPods firmware update, you’ll see a long-awaited new feature in the Settings app: custom EQ.

You now have more control over how your AirPods sound thanks to the new custom EQ controls. In the Settings app, you can adjust the lows, mids, and highs of your AirPods sound.

“AirPods are designed and engineered by Apple to faithfully represent music, TV shows and movies, and calls,” Apple explains. “If you prefer a different sound profile, you can customize how AirPods represent any audio played.”

While adjusting the custom EQ settings, you can play a song from Apple Music right in the Settings app to hear the adjustments in real time.

This isn’t the most advanced equalizer feature out there. It’s a basic, three-band system. Still, it’s a long-awaited AirPods feature that Apple has finally given users—even if most will likely stick with the default levels.

You can find the new custom EQ feature in the AirPods section of the Settings app under the “Audio and Routing” menu. The feature is available on all AirPods with an H2 chip, including AirPods Pro 2, AirPods Pro 3, AirPods 4, and AirPods Max 2.

Other iOS 27 features for AirPods

Here are the other new AirPods features for iOS 27:

Settings app redesign: In iOS 27, Apple has redesigned the AirPods interface in the Settings app. The controls have been reorganized, with separate menus for Hearing Health, Find My, Live Translation, and more.

Adaptive Audio slider: In the Settings app, you now have a slider to further fine-tune Adaptive Audio mode.

GymKit: While GymKit has been around for years, it’s always required an Apple Watch. As my colleague Zac explains, iOS 27 brings the full GymKit experience to iPhone and AirPods Pro 3.

Precision Finding: You can now use Precision Finding in the Find My app on Apple Watch to locate AirPods Pro 3.

Siri AI: When paired to a compatible iPhone, AirPods can interact with Siri AI.

Wrap up

What new AirPods features are you most excited to try? Are you going to try the new custom EQ feature? Let us know down in the comments.

title: Android Auto rolls out game support, no longer in beta
snippet: Google is graduating game support on Android Auto from a limited beta to broad availability, allowing developers to bring games to your car’s display. more…
fullText:
Google is graduating game support on Android Auto from a limited beta to broad availability, allowing developers to bring games to your car’s display.

First available last year, games in Android Auto and Android Automotive bring a bit of interactive fun to the car’s display. While there’s no direct integration with things like the car’s steering wheel, it’s a nice way to add something fun to the biggest screen in your vehicle for times you might be stuck on the side of the road, waiting on an EV to charge, or other times where the vehicle is not moving.

Around 30 games are available on Android Auto today, but that list is likely to start expanding soon.

Google announced this week that game support on Android Auto is no longer in beta, meaning that game support is open to all developers rather than requiring specific approval from Google. 

	

Google says:

Bringing your game to cars lets you reach users in their vehicles during natural downtime, such as while waiting at a charging station or for a curbside order pickup. Today’s milestone means that we’re opening up access so developers can now publish games to the open testing and production tracks on Google Play. In this post, we’ll cover how to adapt your existing Android game for the car screen, focusing on key technical requirements and publishing criteria.

Android games must declare support for Android Auto and Android Automotive OS – they’re separate declarations behind the scenes, and there are many more games that support Android Automotive without Android Auto support as it stands today.

Games on Android Auto should be able to adapt to different display sizes and need to recognize when a vehicle is parked or not – games can only be played if the vehicle is parked. Games can also support controllers on Android Auto and Android Automotive. 

Google’s full documentation on what developers need to do can be found here.

title: Nothing Phone (4a) and (3a) Pro can now join Android 17 open beta
snippet: Right on schedule, Nothing is releasing Nothing OS 5.0 open beta for the Phone (4a), Phone (3a Pro, and Phone (3a) before the company’s official Android 17 release next month. more…
fullText:
Right on schedule, Nothing is releasing Nothing OS 5.0 open beta for the Phone (4a), Phone (3a Pro, and Phone (3a) before the company’s official Android 17 release next month.

The Android 17 package contains a few changes for Nothing phones. It was first released as a beta update for the Nothing Phone (3) with visual changes to the system UI and animations across the board. The update also includes new widgets, updates to the camera app, and a dedicated Glyph app for light controls and features.

You can check out the full changelog in our previous coverage. At its core, it brings Nothing’s devices up to date with the latest version of Android. Of course, this company is known for creating its own spin on both hardware and software.

Right now, though, Nothing is actively rolling out Android 17 beta access to the Nothing Phone (4a), Phone (3a) Pro, and Phone (3a). The update leaves out the Phone (3a) Lite, which is expected to get access later in the year. Users with either of those devices should now be able to access the Nothing OS 5.0 open beta, which puts it on par with the Phone (3).

	

In terms of scheduling, Nothing is right on time. The company posted its release schedule when the first open beta rolled out, and it remains unchanged. The three devices announced today will be followed by the Phone (2a) and Phone (2a) Plus in October.

The same post also notes the Phone (4a) and Phone (3a) series will be pushed to the official Android 17 build in early November. The rollout is expected to end sometime in January 2027.

For the time being, Phone (4a) and (3a) series users should now be able to access Nothing OS 5.0 in its early stages.

title: Samsung has delayed its Android 17 update
snippet: Samsung appears to be delaying the rollout of its Android 17 update, at least slightly, with pushback in some regions. more…
fullText:
Samsung appears to be delaying the rollout of its Android 17 update, at least slightly, with pushback in some regions.

The launch of a stable One UI 9 rollout for Galaxy S26 was first announced last week, with the Android 17-based update landing first on Samsung’s current flagship before expanding to more devices. Samsung explicitly said the rollout was supposed to start on September 16, but it doesn’t appear to have shown up for anyone just yet. 

While the reason is unclear, SammyGuru spotted a sort of confirmation that Samsung has delayed its Android 17 in some capacity.

A press release around the One UI 9 rollout on Samsung’s Newsroom in Thailand noted a rollout date of September 21 originally, but was updated to say September 28, and now appears to have been updated again to remove a specific date altogether, only saying “September 2026” at this point.

	

This isn’t unprecedented; Samsung has had numerous major updates be delayed quietly at the last moment, but it’s certainly not the best start for One UI 9’s rollout. Hopefully, whatever issues are pushing Samsung’s schedule back can be fixed as soon as possible.

title: Adobe Premiere for Android launches for free with layered video editing, YouTube templates
snippet: Months after it arrived on iPhone, Adobe Premiere’s mobile version is now available on Android devices with layered video editing, templates, foldable optimization, and more. more…
fullText:
Months after it arrived on iPhone, Adobe Premiere’s mobile version is now available on Android devices with layered video editing, templates, foldable optimization, and more.

Adobe Premiere Pro is widely recognized as a powerful video editing suite on desktop machines, but Adobe’s last version for mobile devices vanished a while back. Now, Adobe Premiere is once again available on Android, delivering what appears to be a very capable video editor that promises to be a solution across all Android devices.

This is the same app that debuted on iPhone in late 2025, and it brings quite a few features with it.

Some of the key features include:

	

Enhance Audio: Reduce background noise, clean up voiceovers, etc

Multi-track timeline: Manage multiple videos, sound effects, music, etc

Templates: Custom-made templates to speed up editing

Effects: Transitions, creative assets, Adobe Stock integration

Export: Up to 4K editing + export

The app already has wide support of different Android devices and form factors, including optimization for foldable smartphones. There’s also a built-in voice recorder.

Adobe says that more features are coming, including support for Adobe Fonts in creating text overlays, the ability to transfer projects to Premiere Pro on desktop, “beat detection,” cropping, and more. 

The big deal here, though, is that Adobe Premiere for Android is free. You don’t need a Creative Cloud subscription, you don’t need to sit through ads, and there are no watermarks either. Adobe says you can purchase upgrades for “additional generative credits and storage,” but that’s optional.

Requirements for Adobe Premiere on Android include 5GB of RAM or more and Android 13 or newer.

title: The SaaSpocalypse that wasn’t, with Atlassian CEO Mike Cannon-Brookes
snippet: Today, I’m talking with Mike Cannon-Brookes, who is cofounder and CEO of Atlassian. Atlassian is one of those companies that every other company runs on — it makes important platform tools like Jira and Trello that allow people to organize and manage big teams, create shared databases of company information, and generally allow work to happen. As you’ll hear Mike say, all of Atlassian’s products are actually different expressions of a single core platform, which really shapes how Atlassian itself is structured and how those products are built. All of this means Atlassian is also right in the middle of the way AI is changing how all these companies work — AI tools might be able to look at all the different tools and systems you have and just read them for you, making a big migration to Atlassian’s platform less enticing. Or, if you buy the idea of the so-called SaaSpocalypse, AI might just build all of these tools for you, destroying this entire category of businesses. Verge subscribers, don’t forget you get exclusive access to ad-free Decoder wherever you get your podcasts. Head here. Not a subscriber? You can sign up here. Obviously, Mike had a lot of thoughts pushing back on this. So we spent some real time talking about the value of design, human users, how AI is actually increasing the usage of Atlassian’s tools, and what this all looks like a few years from now. Of course, AI has also changed Atlassian. Like so many other tech companies, Atlassian did a round of layoffs earlier this year, with Mike saying he felt the company needed a different “mix of skills.” So I asked Mike what he thinks that mix of skills is and how AI is changing what it means to run a software company. But Mike was also refreshingly direct about what AI can’t do, and he was willing to push back on his own friends like Cloudflare CEO Matthew Prince, who was just on the show talking about AI eliminating what he called “measurement roles.” This was a fun one — and shoutout to Mike, who recorded this from Atlassian home base in Australia, which meant he had a deep conversation about org charts at 5AM. Okay: Atlassian CEO Mike Cannon-Brookes. Here we go. Mike Cannon-Brookes, you’re the co-founder and CEO of Atlassian. Welcome to Decoder. Thanks for having me, man. I am really excited to talk to you. I believe you’re in Australia? Yes. It’s tomorrow for you. What’s going to happen tomorrow? It’s tonight. It’s a great day here. It looks beautiful. It looks like it’s going to be an amazing day. At this point in the AI news cycle, I feel like I can just demand to know what’s going to happen tomorrow, and everyone understands the urgency behind that question. There’s a lot going on with Atlassian. There’s a lot going on with your products. There’s a lot going on in the very concept of SaaS businesses and business processes generally. Let’s start at the very start. I think people know Atlassian. They know Jira. I started my career as a Trello person. Tell people what you think Atlassian is today. Atlassian is a platform that enables businesses to collaborate and manage work across their teams. We connect their business teams and their technology teams to handle the most challenging work problems in a singular platform across any organization that is technologically driven. For any organization that has software and technology as its core competitive advantage, we make a broad platform that allows them to collaborate on content, manage projects, and unleash the knowledge of their teams and organizations across their business, their strategy, operations, all the way through to their service teams in all areas of their business. It’s a very large platform now that we provide. Just in terms of what work is today and what it might be in the future as we add more and more AI to these enterprises, maybe this is too reductive, but I have always thought of Atlassian as a company that makes tools to help teams figure out what they’re going to do tomorrow. Jira is a perfect example of this. You don’t do the software engineering in Jira, but Jira helps you organize large teams of software engineers and file tickets and prioritize problems and tasks. I was a Trello person a long time ago. My goal in life now is to never use any enterprise software. I feel like that’s a sign of true success if you’re just an iPad person in first class. I’m working on it. I’m not saying I’m there yet, but that’s one of my goals. But there was a time when I was the managing editor of The Verge and my job, straightforwardly, was to look at Trello every day and make sure everyone was doing the right thing at the right time. And I’ve always thought of Atlassian as that class of products. We’re going to organize the processes of the company. There’s something about AI that’s changing that. Has that conception of Atlassian changed for you? Is it changing faster because of AI? Understanding what work you have to do at an individual level like Trello, at a team level like Jira, or at an organizational level like our Strategy Collection for large-scale strategy and operations — that is definitely a big part of what we do. Understanding where processes are at — It’s less about work to do than processes. If you think about a business as a system of processes that are put together, everything in a business is some sort of system. It’s a process in the collection of all these, and how well we execute them is what your business is doing. The fundamentals of that haven’t changed. The way those processes run, the number of them running, and how to figure out what’s going on hasn’t changed. We think about Jira as a human reference to work. When we say that, it’s a really interesting term because, as you said, the work is not done in Jira. Developers don’t live in Jira. Marketers don’t live in Jira. Finance people don’t live in Jira. Jira is a workflow engine with highly collaborative parts that enables teams to understand what they, their colleagues, and their broader organization are doing. That’s why agents and AI and other things are going to increase the speed of those processes. In a lot of ways, they will increase the reliability, the quality, and the consistency of output of certain processes. They also put more emphasis on where the humans, the judgment, the intuition, the human bits that are unique, and the initiation come from. It’s our job to make sure that that’s all still understandable so someone can just look at any level of their business and know what the fuck’s going on. What are people doing? Are we successfully doing whatever it is that we’re trying to do, whether that’s service function in a finance sales deal, exception service desk to work out how many exceptions did we give out in sales this quarter, or it’s an engineering team who’s trying to work out, “There’s stuff happening all over the place. What did we build this month? Or what are we going to build next month?” All of those things are incredibly hard to do at scale and volume in a business. One of the more important features of the tools you’ve built is legibility. It’s user experience. You have a big database of exceptions given out by salespeople, and you need to look at a dashboard and see how the company’s doing. Or you have a whole bunch of tasks, and Jira will let you see at various different levels of abstraction how many tasks are being completed at any given time. That was something that was very important for human managers. A lot of the capability unlock of businesses as they added software like the software Atlassian makes is to just be able to see and coordinate more things at a higher scale. The turn that’s coming is that maybe those databases aren’t going to be looked at by human beings anymore, or they’re going to be fed into more synthesized databases, or AI is going to make some other kind of information at different levels of abstraction. I know you’ve got a product called Rovo which feels like the new face of Atlassian in some ways. What’s the path here? What does the end state look like? There’s no doubt AI is going to help with a lot of those processes. There’s no doubt it’s going to pick up some steps in a process. Most businesses at the moment have a process, and they’re using AI to automate 80% of this step. It may not be 80% of the distance. It can be the width. If you think about that sales deal exception process that you just mentioned again there, if AI can take 80% of the exception — say this customer wants 45 days, not 30 days — and we can write a relatively readable document, AI is pretty good at reading the document and saying, “Yep, this one’s fine.” But there’s going to be a customer that needs a lot more complex exceptions. They say, “I want to pay in 90 days in this way, and I want this thing and that thing.” That needs to go to a human for intuition and judgment. So 80% of those may be easier done with AI now because it’s very capable at processing our rules in this particular part of our business, and that’s great. It’ll increase the speed of the process, the quality of it. It doesn’t take away the need to know what’s going on. Someone in the business will still need to know, “How many exceptions did we give?” What happens in most of these areas is businesses find way more ways to make themselves scale and efficient, and they find way more ways to make higher-quality products and services with AI. I see this all the time where they are utilizing AI in ways that people don’t expect. It’s not all about mechanistic efficiency. There’s a huge amount of quality that is able to be measured and understood that was never before. The deal exception process is a good example because it’s actually a very human process. It’s not usually rule-driven. The rule-driven parts are easy. It’s the non-rule-driven parts that are more complicated and require judgment. The business still needs to know, for that process, “Do we need to add more people to this process? Do we need to change it? How much is going through it?” You still have a lot of work to understand the flow of work around an enterprise, which gets more complicated as the flow’s volume goes up a lot. I’m asking because I’m headed towards a series of questions about the supposed SaaSpocalypse, and I’m very curious where you think tool providers like Atlassian fit next to the frontier models are just going to eat more and more capability. Eventually, Claude will just do this for you. You’ll say to Claude, “Run my business for me.” In the backend, Claude will burn a bunch of tokens, and it’ll just do it all for you, which is a promise that many, many people seem to believe in. You’re describing a somewhat different path where the tools get smarter or more capable because of AI, and you’re still adding a lot of human judgment, but at no point is a frontier model just coming and running your entire business for you. If a frontier model is capable of coming and running the entire business for you, if it’s truly running the whole thing, even assuming four or five years worth of increase, you have a relatively simple business. Most businesses aren’t simple. They are global conglomerations of rules, compliance, laws, staff in different places, human inconsistency — which is the same as saying human creativity — that they’re putting it all together to try to deliver products and services for their customers in their industry: healthcare, university, finance, automotive, or whatever the industry is. They’re trying to compete with some other business. They are still going to have a huge number of humans, I would argue more knowledge workers, more developers, in five to 10 years time than today because the ability to do tasks to compete will go up. The bar for competition will go up in almost all these industries. You will still have a huge amount of things to go do. Most of the things that we think are simple will get done for you. That is the history of technology. I’m a big fan of saying AI is just technology. What we can do with spreadsheets, what we can do with the internet, what we can do with ordering goods online… You think, “Once Amazon arrives, we’ll all just never have to go to the shops again.” It doesn’t happen. I heard someone talking about bank branches as an analogy, which I thought was a really good one. Around 2000 when mobile banking came along, everyone thought bank branches were dead. Bank branches started closing down. Everyone wasn’t going to go to their branch anymore. It was a pretty negative place. At least it was in Australia. I’m pretty sure it was in America as well. If you look over the last 10 years, bank branches are increasing. People are like, “Huh, this is a narrative violation. Why is this?” And the answer is bank branches did close down. People did go to internet banking. They did use their mobile app. They don’t go into the branch anymore with a passport to say, “I’d like to send $100 to Nilay, please. Here are his details,” and write them all down. But bank branches have adapted. The reason they’re growing is there is a huge customer service element to a bank branch. The services they provide today are totally different than what they provided 25 years ago due to the technology of the bank and the availability of things. They are much more about helping you with higher-level processes and services than they ever have been. That turns out to be, presumably, profitable for the banks, which is why they’re opening new branches. Bank branches are going up. The things those branches are doing are totally different to what they were 25 years ago. I think you’ll see the same thing with knowledge workers and everything else, that it will still be incredibly important. I don’t see that part changing. I am working my way up to getting Jamie Dimon on the show to find out what happens in all the Chase Bank branches in New York, because I don’t actually know, but we’ll set that aside. Jamie will come on the show. We’ll ask, and we’ll figure it out. One of the reasons I’m asking all these foundational existential questions is to understand how you feel about Atlassian’s relationship to businesses and how businesses might change as we add new technology. I agree with your general framing that automation technology arriving to a business is a pretty familiar phenomenon, but there’s something else going on with AI that is either making that faster or more dramatic. It’s obviously happening to your business as well. You’re the CEO of Atlassian, and you’ve made some changes around AI. I want to ask you the Decoder questions now. How many people is Atlassian today? And how is it structured? We are, I think publicly, 12,000-13,000-odd people around the world. We are structured globally, I would say. We are “Team Anywhere.” Employees have the choice to come into an office or not. About 60 percent of people come in three days a week or more. About 25 percent of people don’t come in a single day per week. We run as a globally distributed company as we have done since the start. When you start in Australia and San Francisco, you kind of get used to the Pacific Ocean being a little bit of a distribution. This was before Zoom. We used to have these giant Polycom systems in meeting rooms. We don’t have those anymore. Technological progress is nice. We have customers all around the world. We have staff all around the world. We are structured functionally, I guess you would say, with a lot of matrices internally. I don’t know if that’s the answer you’re looking for. No, that’s absolutely the answer I’m looking for. What do you mean by “functionally with a lot of matrices”? We have a CRO. We have a CFO. We have two CTOs at the moment. We have two large product groups, each of which has a CTO and a chief product officer, one in the enterprise and emerging side and one in the future of teamwork side. Our products are organized into collections. We have collections of apps that are all built on a single platform. Well over half of our R&D is on the platform. The apps are increasingly a smaller amount of the proportional total investment in building. More and more is on the singular Atlassian platform. Customers hire us as a platform across their business to get work done, not for a single application. That requires a matrix internally. We don’t have salespeople per product, if you want to think about it that way. The sales, customer success, and the FDEs are all customer-related motions. They’re organized as per the customers and their geographies and their size and scale. Then we obviously have to have designers and product managers on particular products who care about the purpose of a product, so you end up instantly with the matrix between how the customers are organized and how the products are organized. We have a giant platform. We have the technical platform that runs across all the products. It’s a very large platform team. We then have finance and talent and other things that are also broad processes. Naturally, you end up with collaborative areas that you have to get together, and we manage that through our operating processes. Do you use the Atlassian platform to run Atlassian? We do. We run entirely on the Atlassian platform. I used to say we’re the number one user — we’re not anymore — of our strategy and operations products to understand what our business is focusing on, what our large-scale goals are, how the people, the investments, and the technical systems all come together, and what is going right and wrong across all of those. We are a big believer in our Strategy Collection to operate a large-scale business. One of my favorite questions to ask enterprise software CEOs is how much they personally use the enterprise software. How much do you personally use your products? An awful lot. What’s your number one feature request for your teams? My number one feature request is usually continual UI congruence. I guess that’s the category that people would put it in. I’m a bit of a stickler for design and consistency. We want to achieve eventual consistency in design, in which we’ve come a huge distance in the last five years. In the last two years, we’ve been truly world-class at doing it. That’s usually my biggest area where I use a lot of our products on a regular basis. As such, I’m moving around the platform, and I’m looking for ways where this thing over here happens this way. They do it better over there. We’re trying to achieve that eventual consistency across a large product surface area. I use Dia, our web browser. I think 96 to 97 percent of Atlassian now uses Dia on a regular basis. I mean, that’s a daily basis, so I literally spend many, many, many hours of the day on it. We are building a web browser for ourselves because we’ve reached the point that we feel, “This thing should just be better for knowledge workers.” We’ve already built, I would argue, the best browser for knowledge workers in the world, and it’s getting much, much, much better. Keep watching this space. So, yes, I would say there’s no 24-hour period that goes by where I don’t use one of our products. I doubt there’s a six-hour period that goes by where I don’t use one of our products at the moment. I want to talk about Dia in a second, because I’m very curious about that acquisition. Obviously, we covered The Browser Company very deeply at The Verge. That was a big acquisition for you guys. Setting that aside for just one second, one of the things I’m particularly curious about here is the distinction between the platform and the products that run on the platform. Again, maybe this is just reductive, but it sounds like there’s a big layer of capability, and the products are expressions of those capabilities in different ways, but they’re all running on the same core platform. Is that how you think about it? Yes, absolutely. Yes. We have to build a singular R&D platform, whether that’s how we talk to AI gateways, whether that’s how chat works, whether that’s how automation and identity and logging and governance and compliance and content classification work, whether that’s how our home and our search engine work. There are many, many more technical capabilities that have to be shared. Then you have all of the next layer up, and customers want that to work the same. It doesn’t matter if I’m in Confluence or Jira or Loom or the Service Collection, automation shouldn’t be different per place in the world. That’s very expensive. It’s very hard. It takes a lot of time, but it delivers a huge amount of customer value and loyalty. Most vendors don’t try to do that. They literally don’t try. Then you have a layer up, which is important, which is the consistency of operation and how content can be mixed. Operations and processes can be mixed across applications. If I open a Confluence page inside of Jira, I want that to feel like a Confluence page, but I want it to be inside of Jira. I don’t want to leave Jira to open it. I just want to read it, close it, keep going. There’s a lot of UI layer, a sort of recomposability, if you want to think about it that way. Lastly, each application has to do its job. If you blend enterprise software together, you end up in a world of hell. People have tried this many times. You want a tool to do a job. You want to pick up a screwdriver or a hammer or saw and feel like that thing’s going to do the thing you hired it to do. The interface is designed to help you do that task. That’s where there is a difference in the interface layer and the interaction layer, between those tools. The combination of those is where a lot of our design challenges live. For example, our chat layer, Rovo, is amazing. I would argue it’s one of the best, if not very close to the best enterprise chat products in the world. Our customers continually say that. “How come you’re better than insert-famous-brand-here?” There are a lot of reasons why we perform better in evaluations and testing with Rovo. It’s not because we make a foundational LLM, I think, which is the flaw of thinking. However, using Rovo inside a product, if you’re going to Rovo for the sake of Rovo, is awesome. You have a question to ask, you want to search across everything, fine, you go to a particular interface. If you’re inside of Loom or Jira or the Service Collection and you just want to open up chat, ask a question, you want it to understand the context you’re in, but you want that operation to be consistent across the platform. That’s what we’re striving to deliver to customers. One of my constant tropes on the show is that if you describe to me your org chart, I can tell you 80% of your problems. The structure of the company leads to some kind of natural politics in some kind of way. The tension between “we have products that are designed to do a job” and “we have a platform that contains the core capabilities” is pretty well known. Mm-hmm. Maybe your product teams are going to desire platform capabilities that don’t exist yet or they will desire different platform capabilities from one another. How do you break those ties? How do you make those calls? We have a number of ways that we are different and we try to do that. First, I would say most importantly, we have a platform-centric CEO and co-founder who thinks in terms of platforms. Thinking in Systems is my favorite book, man. I have a copy on every desk. You have to put the platform first collectively, and then you go solve a bunch of problems. That does not mean genericism wins, but it does mean when you make trade-offs, you have to spend the extra effort and time to make it platform centric, to make it work. And that is a forever task. It helps to have a CEO, if you think about the referee across all the functions, that’s platform centric. They know where I’m going to land and so we’re going to end up there. Secondly, we have design as a very, very senior role. We have a massive investment in design. Our chief design officer reports to me, sits on our executive team. We now have three, four, five former chief design officers in the business from other very large businesses, some larger than us. We have a huge investment in design and experience. Especially in the AI era, that’s getting ever more important actually, much as Claude Design or something would tell you the opposite. I don’t think so. I actually think [when it comes to] design and the experience of software, if the cost of building goes down, the quality and differentiation is on the experience and the design, and that’s not something that’s easy to do. That requires a huge amount of taste and judgment. Lastly, I think we aren’t afraid to put things together in unusual ways in the organization where we need to solve problems. The latest example of that probably is our internal IT and engineering function now reports to our chief people officer and I’ve combined those two roles, which is unusual. “Why is HR running IT? Chrome and Safari are built the way they are because they have to cater to everyone from five-year-olds to 100-year-olds, who are doing fewer work-related knowledge tasks and are doing more browsing and entertainment and other tasks. That doesn’t mean that someone who’s a knowledge worker in a corporate job isn’t looking at YouTube or Facebook sometimes, but it’s not the purpose of their job. We believe we can build a better browsing experience, a better work experience. One of the pitches we had for the product is we’re not building a browser, we’re building a doer. It’s a totally different thing. We’re helping you do things. We’re not helping you browse passively, and hence why there are tabs and split screens and pin tabs and groups and AI and dynamic tab groups. Live tab groups as we have of the documents you have is a great example. Our documents live tab group in Dia shows you the documents. It will automatically open and close tabs if you want to think about it that way, for you across any content application, Google Drive, Confluence, SharePoint. Any application you use that has documents, if someone comments or shares a document with you, the tab automatically gets opened by your web browser. And if you’re done with it somewhere else, it automatically gets closed by your web browser because that is the set of documents you’re currently working on. Same for pull requests or anything like this. Then we add AI over the top. AI lets us change how we use these knowledge applications in insane ways. The browser has your entire history of what you’ve done. It has skills, it has an ability to run AI. You can use Dia to make Minesweeper, and you can use Dia to make Minesweeper out of the tasks that you did in the last week. It’ll go start a computer underneath the browser. It’ll run a bunch of code generation. It’ll create an application for you that plays Minesweeper based on the tasks you have completed in the last week. Now, I don’t think that’s a very useful application, but the fact that it can do it is amazing. The most popular feature of Dia is the Morning Brief. People are blown away and often suspicious about how we can understand what you need to do today with a fidelity and a design quality and an experience that makes it a joyful experience when it pops up every morning. Mine opened about 45 minutes ago. That is a design challenge. That is an amazing team of designers that are thinking about our most-used application surface area and reimagining it for knowledge workers and for the AI era simultaneously, with access to every SaaS application that you have open on your computer in a way that corporate security is going to say, “This is a good idea and I trust it.” That is the mission that we embarked on a year ago, that The Browser Company embarked on three years ago, and it’s usable today. It’s coming out on Windows any day now, it’s in beta on Windows, general availability is very soon, and it’s used on the Mac by a huge number of people on a daily basis and only increasing. Like I said, we’ve been covering that product for a long time. I’m glad it found a home with you all. Let me just push you a little bit on moving up the stack to the next level of user interface. You could argue that already happened with web browsers. Windows was disrupted by the very presence of the web browser. The iMac was only successful because the most interesting thing you could do with a computer at that time was go on the web. The presence of the web browser on the Mac allowed a bunch of applications to move away from Windows binaries to being web apps and then cloud apps and now productivity apps in the cloud. The web as an application environment is probably more vital and important than ever before. It is the thing you’re describing. It’s where all the applications live and a custom web browser designed to do work is very important. At the same time, I would just say, didn’t that already happen? Are you actually moving up the stack or are you just building a more custom web browser, or is AI changing that in some other way? AI is changing that. AI is giving us the ability to help you understand what work you have to do, not just your browsing history. One of the most powerful things about AI that people don’t broadly understand is… An LLM’s ability to generate content is well known. I can say, “Tell me a dad joke,” and it spits one out. It streams out tokens. What is more important for application vendors like us, people who are trying to make tools and products and solutions for customers, is the ability to read text, not write it, but read it, because we can understand meaning for the first time ever. We can understand what a page or a comment or a piece of text is about. Then we can make application-level choices, which we never could do beforehand. Word didn’t know what document you were writing. When it said, “It looks like you’re writing a letter,” it was really shithouse and it was a terrible experience. Now it can actually tell with super high fidelity, “Are you writing a letter, a PhD? Is it a high school essay or a university essay?” It can adapt and change its interface. The ability of Dia and AI is to understand what it is that you are browsing, what it is that you are doing, to be able to reach into applications to get content and to pull it back to give you tools to manage your day. The Morning Brief looks across your calendar and your messaging tools and your document tools to tell you what it is you have today in a very intelligent manner, the way it would be if you gave me all your content and said, “Spend the days.” Now it reads millions of words in order to generate that and it has a lot of smarts to give you a very simple experience of the most important things you need to do today that are totally different from anybody else on the planet. That requires a lot of AI to do and it requires connections to all of your SaaS apps. The browser’s logged into all those apps so it can do that. It happens locally, it doesn’t happen in the cloud, it happens on your machine. That is something that we could never do before to understand, “Of these 10 documents you looked at yesterday, here’s the one you need to do today because I know in your calendar you got to do this tomorrow, you got to do these things. This is the most important thing for us to do today, and let me help you get started on that task. Let me draft some notes for you. Let me help you with that document. Let me help you do things.” That is something that was never ever possible beforehand. Lastly, it understands the people you interact with. People are left out of so many of these conversations and equations. You can think of Dia as having a mini CRM that is constantly updated based on your browsing habits. It’s a weird analogy, but it’s effectively what it’s doing, one of the many things it’s doing inside the browser, which is why its answers are so good. It knows that you and I don’t know each other very well. It knows I know my head of engineering extremely well. If that person asks me for something, because it’s maintaining a constant context graph of people relationships across every single one of your SaaS applications into duplicating and normalizing and using AI, all of that helps to understand what tasks are actually important to me. It can look at LinkedIn and see who you are and say, “That interview prep you got to do today, you should put that up your stack. Nilay’s an important person.” It does all of that for you, and help you- Can you put that in the Dia system prompt so people know when they come to talk to me? Just hard code that in there, you got to prioritize. We’ll see if we know some people. But it’s hard, and the experience, none of that should need to be known by somebody using Dia. The experience should just be a beautiful, joyful way to start your day. We want to leave you with more sense of calm, control, comfort about your day, not stress about AI. Leave that to us to do really well and we just give you the answers that you need from your tools and applications. It also does not mean you use less of those tools and applications. I don’t use Dia and stop using Slack. I don’t use Dia and stop using Confluence. It’s helping me understand which thing I need to do next by understanding what’s inside those things. By cross-referencing with my LinkedIn and my Salesforce and my Microsoft Teams conversations and meeting transcripts, but it’s doing that all for me in the morning and during the day to be able to say, “Here’s what you have to do next. Here’s the most important thing,” and providing an interface to allow me to organize and group those tasks in ways that hopefully are bordering on joyful. They’re beautiful and simple experiences and there are so many lovely touches in Dia that just make it a joy to use every day. We’re pushing that mission really hard. Can I add a wild card? It seems very obvious to me that you have a very clear view of how AI should work in enterprise and how work should get done using your tools, your tools enhanced by AI, your tools expressed in your browser. There’s focus there, and I appreciate that. On the other side of the house, on the consumer side, my argument has been that reason people hate AI and they’re mad about it is a little bit that the doomers have said there’s a 10% chance we’re all going to die and all of our jobs are going away, but there are also no great products. There’s not as much coherence and focus as I’m hearing from you in the enterprise context. Do you think that there’s some great consumer AI product in the offing that has the kind of focus that you have in enterprise? Because that seems like the missing piece for me. Yes and no. Yes, if you look at the history of technological disruptions, the products that came through the disruption often aren’t linearly related to the disruption. If you think about the smartphone era — and we all pick up our smartphones 100 times a day, don’t tell me you don’t. When the iPhone came out, we were all excited by little bits and pieces. We did not think, man, that camera thing’s going to lead to this Instagram phenomenon. We did not think the GPS is going to lead to Uber and so I can take transportation. The products that came as a result of the technology shift. The iPhone is an amazing business, don’t get me wrong, but the services and changes to life didn’t come from the iPhone. They came from the apps that it enabled, like Uber and Instagram and whatever else you like on the mobile phone. It can be a game, it can be anything. Those take a while for people to play with the form factor to understand the bits. Uber didn’t come along until the iPhone 6, because all it needed was to get better and then someone said, “Wait, we can take a car with a phone and it’ll just show up?” Yeah, we can show you where the car is and we can build enough trust and we can build a whole service layer. I suspect one part of it is in AI, we need to keep playing, and I know the Muse team pretty well. That’s an amazing example of an application. There are many, many more of these things. There’s a company that one of my kids loves called Tolan which makes these Hollywood AI agent chatbot things with personality. Someone from technology would say, “Ah, that’s just OpenClaw with some skin on it.” Kids say, “This is a character that I can interact with.” It’s an amazing psychology Hollywood game character. These sort of applications we’re just starting to see. It’s going to be an incredibly exciting five years of those sets of applications. I suspect it takes way longer than we think to understand, get to GPT-6, get to understanding memory and harnesses and putting all these things together. It probably won’t be OpenClaw, it’ll be some version of how an agent surfaces in a certain area of life. So yes, the products are still coming in the consumer space. Secondly, I think the “no” part of the answer is that AI is not a product, it’s a technology. It’s a piece of technology. If it just makes everything about your life a bit better, you won’t even notice you’re using AI, and actually, that’s the beauty of it. You can use Dia all day long and not realize how much AI it’s doing. Just like the Morning Brief thing, it’s really good. I look at it every morning, it’s one of the most highly engaged features we’ve ever built. And it just tells you, “Here are the three things I think you need to do today. Here’s what your day looks like. You want me to help you prep for this thing?” And you say, “Yeah, help me prep for that thing.” You don’t need to know it’s AI. We don’t tell you it’s AI. We’re purposefully not trying to hide it, it’s not secret, but you need to have a great experience. You don’t care there’s an LLM and tokens and gateways and massive amount of technology going on behind the scenes. You just want to know what the three things you have to do this morning are. And if you build trust in it, that’s great. The hard part when you mention the data centers and stuff is that people want those experiences and they’re going to be very joyful and very contented and more calm and happy about the experiences they’re getting. They’re just not going to be using AI. I tell this to people here all the time, every time you take a photo on the iPhone, there is an insane amount of AI processing going on to make that photo look good. Insane amount. And photos look amazing on my phone compared to what they did 10 or 20 years ago. Do I need to know that? Nope. I want to point at my kid, snap a photo, and I want it to look good. That’s great technology, when it disappears. That’s what it should be in the enterprise or for consumers. There’s no reason people in the enterprise should put up with shitty technology. That’s consistent, but it’s not going to be necessarily knowable that I’m using AI. It’s just going to be an amazing product experience like Dia that says, “Here are the three things you got to do today.” And it gets it right. Even beginning to describe the conversations I’ve had with the Apple camera team about the use of AI on those photos is a full other hour of this show that we do not have time for. Mike, this was a great conversation. What’s next for Atlassian? What should people be looking for? We have a massive set of announcements in, I’m scared to say, a bit over a week, 10 days. We have a biannual conference, our Team 26 EU in Amsterdam in 10 days’ time, announcements in every collection. You will no doubt see lots of AI features that are magical and disappear. You don’t need to know that you’re using them. Dia launches, Teamwork Collection launches. A lot of fantastic Loom features. We haven’t talked about Loom, massive in the AI era. We have so much on Loom’s agentic use, some of which has been online. Kudos to the partnership with the Cursor team, we built some amazing Cursor and Loom features. Really exciting stuff coming up in 10 days’ time. We will have to have you back very soon to talk about what happens with enterprise software in just one year’s time, because I’m confident it’s going to change. Thank you so much for being on Decoder. Thank you for having me. Thanks, man. Questions or comments? Hit us up at decoder@theverge.com. We really do read every email!
fullText:
Today, I’m talking with Mike Cannon-Brookes, who is cofounder and CEO of Atlassian.

Atlassian is one of those companies that every other company runs on — it makes important platform tools like Jira and Trello that allow people to organize and manage big teams, create shared databases of company information, and generally allow work to happen. As you’ll hear Mike say, all of Atlassian’s products are actually different expressions of a single core platform, which really shapes how Atlassian itself is structured and how those products are built.

All of this means Atlassian is also right in the middle of the way AI is changing how all these companies work — AI tools might be able to look at all the different tools and systems you have and just read them for you, making a big migration to Atlassian’s platform less enticing. Or, if you buy the idea of the so-called SaaSpocalypse, AI might just build all of these tools for you, destroying this entire category of businesses.

Verge subscribers, don’t forget you get exclusive access to ad-free Decoder wherever you get your podcasts. Head here. Not a subscriber? You can sign up here.

Obviously, Mike had a lot of thoughts pushing back on this. So we spent some real time talking about the value of design, human users, how AI is actually increasing the usage of Atlassian’s tools, and what this all looks like a few years from now.

Of course, AI has also changed Atlassian. Like so many other tech companies, Atlassian did a round of layoffs earlier this year, with Mike saying he felt the company needed a different “mix of skills.” So I asked Mike what he thinks that mix of skills is and how AI is changing what it means to run a software company.

But Mike was also refreshingly direct about what AI can’t do, and he was willing to push back on his own friends like Cloudflare CEO Matthew Prince, who was just on the show talking about AI eliminating what he called “measurement roles.” This was a fun one — and shoutout to Mike, who recorded this from Atlassian home base in Australia, which meant he had a deep conversation about org charts at 5AM.

Okay: Atlassian CEO Mike Cannon-Brookes. Here we go.

Mike Cannon-Brookes, you’re the co-founder and CEO of Atlassian. Welcome to Decoder.

Thanks for having me, man.

I am really excited to talk to you. I believe you’re in Australia?

Yes.

It’s tomorrow for you. What’s going to happen tomorrow?

It’s tonight. It’s a great day here. It looks beautiful. It looks like it’s going to be an amazing day.

At this point in the AI news cycle, I feel like I can just demand to know what’s going to happen tomorrow, and everyone understands the urgency behind that question. There’s a lot going on with Atlassian. There’s a lot going on with your products. There’s a lot going on in the very concept of SaaS businesses and business processes generally.

Let’s start at the very start. I think people know Atlassian. They know Jira. I started my career as a Trello person. Tell people what you think Atlassian is today.

Atlassian is a platform that enables businesses to collaborate and manage work across their teams. We connect their business teams and their technology teams to handle the most challenging work problems in a singular platform across any organization that is technologically driven.

For any organization that has software and technology as its core competitive advantage, we make a broad platform that allows them to collaborate on content, manage projects, and unleash the knowledge of their teams and organizations across their business, their strategy, operations, all the way through to their service teams in all areas of their business. It’s a very large platform now that we provide.

Just in terms of what work is today and what it might be in the future as we add more and more AI to these enterprises, maybe this is too reductive, but I have always thought of Atlassian as a company that makes tools to help teams figure out what they’re going to do tomorrow. Jira is a perfect example of this. You don’t do the software engineering in Jira, but Jira helps you organize large teams of software engineers and file tickets and prioritize problems and tasks.

I was a Trello person a long time ago. My goal in life now is to never use any enterprise software. I feel like that’s a sign of true success if you’re just an iPad person in first class. I’m working on it. I’m not saying I’m there yet, but that’s one of my goals.

But there was a time when I was the managing editor of The Verge and my job, straightforwardly, was to look at Trello every day and make sure everyone was doing the right thing at the right time. And I’ve always thought of Atlassian as that class of products. We’re going to organize the processes of the company.

There’s something about AI that’s changing that. Has that conception of Atlassian changed for you? Is it changing faster because of AI?

Understanding what work you have to do at an individual level like Trello, at a team level like Jira, or at an organizational level like our Strategy Collection for large-scale strategy and operations — that is definitely a big part of what we do.

Understanding where processes are at — It’s less about work to do than processes. If you think about a business as a system of processes that are put together, everything in a business is some sort of system. It’s a process in the collection of all these, and how well we execute them is what your business is doing. The fundamentals of that haven’t changed. The way those processes run, the number of them running, and how to figure out what’s going on hasn’t changed.

We think about Jira as a human reference to work. When we say that, it’s a really interesting term because, as you said, the work is not done in Jira. Developers don’t live in Jira. Marketers don’t live in Jira. Finance people don’t live in Jira. Jira is a workflow engine with highly collaborative parts that enables teams to understand what they, their colleagues, and their broader organization are doing. That’s why agents and AI and other things are going to increase the speed of those processes. In a lot of ways, they will increase the reliability, the quality, and the consistency of output of certain processes.

They also put more emphasis on where the humans, the judgment, the intuition, the human bits that are unique, and the initiation come from. It’s our job to make sure that that’s all still understandable so someone can just look at any level of their business and know what the fuck’s going on. What are people doing? Are we successfully doing whatever it is that we’re trying to do, whether that’s service function in a finance sales deal, exception service desk to work out how many exceptions did we give out in sales this quarter, or it’s an engineering team who’s trying to work out, “There’s stuff happening all over the place. What did we build this month? Or what are we going to build next month?” All of those things are incredibly hard to do at scale and volume in a business.

One of the more important features of the tools you’ve built is legibility. It’s user experience. You have a big database of exceptions given out by salespeople, and you need to look at a dashboard and see how the company’s doing. Or you have a whole bunch of tasks, and Jira will let you see at various different levels of abstraction how many tasks are being completed at any given time. 

That was something that was very important for human managers. A lot of the capability unlock of businesses as they added software like the software Atlassian makes is to just be able to see and coordinate more things at a higher scale.

The turn that’s coming is that maybe those databases aren’t going to be looked at by human beings anymore, or they’re going to be fed into more synthesized databases, or AI is going to make some other kind of information at different levels of abstraction. I know you’ve got a product called Rovo which feels like the new face of Atlassian in some ways.

What’s the path here? What does the end state look like?

There’s no doubt AI is going to help with a lot of those processes. There’s no doubt it’s going to pick up some steps in a process.
