title: Anker’s 25W MagSafe 3-in-1 packs active cooling in a travel-sized design [Hands-on]
snippet: If you’re rocking an iPhone 16 or newer, you might be interested in a Qi2.2 charger to take full advantage of the 25W MagSafe charging speeds that your phone can support. Anker’s new 25W Prime MagSafe 3-in-1 is one of many great options, and it comes in an excellent portable design. more…
fullText:
If you’re rocking an iPhone 16 or newer, you might be interested in a Qi2.2 charger to take full advantage of the 25W MagSafe charging speeds that your phone can support. Anker’s new 25W Prime MagSafe 3-in-1 is one of many great options, and it comes in an excellent portable design.

Impressions

The big trend of the latter half of 2025 was bringing 25W Qi2.2 to every single wireless charging accessory possible, and that’s continued through 2026. Anker is kicking things off with a new portable MagSafe 3-in-1 that packs 25W Qi2.2 support into a very portable design.

With 25W of wireless charging, active cooling is practically a necessity. Nearly every 25W charger on the market integrates it, and the new Anker foldable 3-in-1 is no exception.

In the box, you get a 45W charge brick and USB-C cable – providing ample power to charge your iPhone, AirPods, and Apple Watch all at once. With this stand, you can charge an iPhone 18 Pro to 50% in just 27 minutes.

Remember MagSafe Duo? If you were someone who really enjoyed that product before Apple killed it off, you’ll likely enjoy this one. It has extremely similar portability characteristics, but comes with two key benefits: it can serve as a stand, and it can charge three devices at once instead of two.

One neat (though totally unnecessary) feature on this charger is that the Apple Watch charger is spring-loaded. It does fold inwards while you have the charger compacted, but when you’re ready to unfold everything, you just need to press downward on it and it springs outward. I thought that was pretty neat, and helps justify the premium price tag that this product demands.

Wrap up

All in all, if you want a nice MagSafe 3-in-1 charger that can easily work for travel, this new Anker offering is a great choice. Since it includes active cooling, it actually charges your iPhone rather quickly without any of the overheating or other negative side affects that wireless charging can sometimes have.

title: Maritime intelligence startup Quartermaster raises another $140M
snippet: The tech enables real-time awareness for what Quartermaster calls the “largest blind spot on Earth.”
fullText:
Arlington, Virginia-based startup Quartermaster in May closed a $43 million Series A around its idea of using weather-hardened sensors to capture data and generate insights about maritime activity. That idea has proven popular, because Quartermaster has already closed a much larger Series B, bringing in $140 million this time.

Founder and CEO Neil Sobin said the round was preempted by software-focused venture firm Insight Partners, and the interest in what Quartermaster is building was helped by the war in Iran and the shipping chaos it’s caused.

“I think we we’ve gained huge amounts of conviction in the core thesis,” Sobin said in an exclusive interview. “A big part of the story for us this year was, events in the world drive that clarity and drive that conviction and urgency, and when you see that, you gotta seize the opportunity.”

About $100 million of the Series B came from Insight and new investor, defense-focused firm Overmatch Ventures, as well as existing backers like First Round Capital. The remaining $40 million came in the form of a debt facility from investment bank Stifel.

“Quartermaster is building a distributed network for the ocean, where reliable, real-time data has been difficult to come by,” Nick Sinai, managing director at Insight Partners, said in a statement to TechCrunch. “The team’s execution and the strong demand for maritime data and awareness made this an investment we wanted to lead, and we’re proud to back Neil and the team as they scale to meet the opportunity with commercial fleets.”

Quartermaster’s hardware, which it calls “SmartMast,” is a fairly straightforward setup. The startup integrates cameras and radios into a package that’s mounted on a ship’s mast, and can capture and relay real-time maritime data. This allows governments, shipping companies and insurance providers to know far more than the current standard of AIS, or the “automatic identification system,” which is more or less just a series of location pings.

This real-time awareness data creates all kinds of opportunities for what Quartermaster calls the “largest blind spot on Earth.” Everything from helping ships avoid collisions, to better understanding congestion in shipping lanes, to rescuing lost mariners is on the table. Sobin said each SmartMast records tens of gigabytes per day, and the startup and its customers are still finding new uses for the data being captured.

“There isn’t a lot of prior art in maritime AI, and so it’s been exciting to, one, have our own source of data,” he said. “But two, there’s just so much low hanging fruit that we’ve been knocking down this summer in what you can start to build and then deliver value for our customers on.”

Sobin said the startup spends a lot of time engaging with people across the maritime industry — and not just vessel owners and operators — in order to find out what they want out of this technology.

“This is an ignored field. Mariners around the world have been ignored by technology for a really long time, and so when they meet us, they’re so excited, because they’re like: ‘Oh, I have so many ideas, let’s work on them’,” he said.

More than 650 vessels are now equipped with SmartMast in 25 countries, Sobin said, and the startup has shipped over 800 to customers. That gap is largely driven by the fact that Quartermaster is about to start deploying the SmartMast system to entire fleets, a sign that early adopters are really buying into the idea. 

Quartermaster has had to hustle to keep up with demand, Sobin said. The startup has doubled its manufacturing capacity and continues to tweak its design so its hardware can be manufactured at a quicker clip.

“We know we can do this, and we are seeing a lot of proof that tells us we’re really onto something massive and important in the world,” Sobin said. “So, what do you do when you have that position? You run faster and you move faster and you double down on that strategy.”

title: iPhone 18 Pro one week later: Zero compromises
snippet: I’ve been using iPhone 18 Pro for the past week after a full year as an iPhone Air user. And while there are advantages with each model, my main takeaway about iPhone 18 Pro so far is that it has zero compromises. Here’s what I mean. more…
fullText:
I’ve been using iPhone 18 Pro for the past week after a full year as an iPhone Air user. And while there are advantages with each model, my main takeaway about iPhone 18 Pro so far is that it has zero compromises. Here’s what I mean.

iPhone 18 Pro: The best camera system, battery life, and performance

If you want to buy a new iPhone, chances are the iPhone 18 Pro is a strong contender.

I’ve had mine for a week now, a Burgundy model that replaced my iPhone Air. And despite loving the Air a lot, it’s hard to match Apple’s no-compromise approach to the iPhone 18 Pro.

Cameras are better and far more versatile on iPhone 18 Pro compared to the Air. Telephoto and Ultra Wide lenses are great for specific use cases, but even the Main camera is better on iPhone 18 Pro.

Battery life is similarly impressive. I generally found the iPhone Air’s battery good enough for everyday use, and only needed to charge mid-day occasionally. But with iPhone 18 Pro I don’t even have to think about battery.

Performance is fantastic too. The A20 Pro chip makes everything on the iPhone feel fast, and I’ve even noticed a more responsive Siri AI. Thanks to the vapor chamber, I haven’t had any issues of overheating either, which the Air sometimes struggled with.

I’m not a pro photographer, and if you want battery tests or performance benchmarks, my colleague Chance’s iPhone 18 Pro review has you covered. But after a week with iPhone 18 Pro, that word “best” keeps coming back to me.

iPhone 18 Pro (and Pro Max) pack the absolute best camera system Apple makes, have the best battery life, and perform better than any other models. I’ve even noticed smaller improvements: the better built-in speakers and Dynamic Island upgrades are highlights.

There are measurable differences in all these areas, but I also appreciate just knowing my iPhone has the “best” Apple offers in key areas that matter most. There’s no wondering: would these pictures of my family look better if I used a different iPhone? Would this slowdown have happened?

All the positives of iPhone 18 Pro aside though, I’ll admit that I’m still very intrigued by the forthcoming iPhone Duo.

iPhone Duo, like iPhone Air, will be compromised but so compelling

The iPhone Air and iPhone Duo share a lot in common. Besides having similar design traits, they also both have shortcomings.

Like my iPhone Air, the iPhone Duo will have a worse camera system than iPhone 18 Pro. Battery might be comparable but definitely worse than the Pro Max, and I suspect sustained performance will lag a bit too. iPhone Duo will also lack Face ID and the Action button.

Yet despite these compromises, I’m very excited to get my hands on the device. 

That’s because it offers a lot of compelling innovations not found in iPhone 18 Pro. The foldable form factor represents arguably the biggest iPhone hardware change ever.

I’ve been enjoying my iPhone 18 Pro a lot. But guess what happened when I picked up the iPhone Air the other day?

I instantly said, “Wow.”

Here’s my iPhone 18 Pro Max review:

Do not buy an iPhone Air unless you want to immediately return every other phone forever.

— Ben Thompson (@benthompson) September 21, 2026

The Air’s thinness had become the norm for me after a year of use. But several days into using iPhone 18 Pro, I was able to find fresh appreciation for how futuristic the Air feels. And I suspect iPhone Duo will evoke similar feelings—not just for its design, but its utility too.

	

I’m excited to have an iPad-like experience with the iPhone that fits in my pocket. That’s true despite being admittedly torn about the downsides the Duo will bring.

The days of Apple offering a single “best” iPhone are gone. If you want a model with zero compromises, iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max seem fantastic. But for something more futuristic and unique, I still can’t wait to try iPhone Duo.

Where do you stand on iPhone 18 Pro vs. iPhone Duo? Let us know in the comments.

title: Google says Gemini 4 release is coming ‘as soon as possible’
snippet: As its rivals continue to iterate quickly, Google has confirmed that its Gemini 4 flagship AI model is nearing release and that it is coming “as soon as possible.” more…
fullText:
As its rivals continue to iterate quickly, Google has confirmed that its Gemini 4 flagship AI model is nearing release and that it is coming “as soon as possible.”

Google DeepMind chief Koray Kavukcuoglu confirmed to The Information at the publication’s AI Agenda Live Summit this week that its next flagship Gemini model, Gemini 4, has entered “post-training,” a phase in which the model’s behavior is refined ahead of a public release. This includes safety testing and implementing guardrails, with internal testing underway using Gemini 4 to power Antigravity.

In other words, Google is getting closer to the release of Gemini 4.

Kavukcuoglu explained:

	

Our intention is to, like—as soon as possible—to release an early post-training output because we see the results and we are excited… [to] continue the fast-paced iterations.

He adds that he hopes the model will be released “much earlier” than the end of 2026, but a specific timeline was not shared.

	

The update comes just days after Anthropic and OpenAI have both launched major updates to their respective flagship AI models in recent weeks. Responding to the idea that Google has “fallen behind,” Kavukcuoglu said that “I have the utmost trust in the team” and that “in my mind, it’s a certainty that we are always gonna be at the frontier.”

Google’s last major flagship model release was in November 2025 with Gemini 3 Pro, followed by Gemini 3.1 Pro in February 2026. There have been several updates to Flash and other models in the time since, most recently with Gemini 3.8 Flash. Google teased Gemini 3.5 Pro over the Summer, but never ended up releasing the model, and this week’s conversation with The Information sheds no light on whether or not that model will be released – Kavukcuoglu said that Google “took a little bit of a step back” to focus on its Flash models instead, but that the current focus is on releasing Gemini 4.

Speaking on AGI, a common conversation around other major AI model updates, Kavukcuoglu says that “the conversation is more about are we able to build intelligent agents that we can trust.”

title: Online CVS Shoppers Might Be Able to Cash In on a $20.5 Million Settlement
snippet: The pharmacy chain denies wrongdoing, but is settling anyway.
fullText:
Popular pharmacy chain CVS has been hit with a lawsuit that alleges the company sold data from customers who shopped on its websites (cvs.com and cvshealth.com) or the mobile app. 

The lawsuit alleges that CVS disclosed private health information, browsing data and more from users to advertising company Criteo and other third parties, though the pharmacy denies any wrongdoing. It has settled to the tune of $20.5 million to avoid additional expenses by continuing the lawsuit and other business disruptions. 

Email notifications (PDF) for potential class members were sent out earlier in September, but the deadline to submit the claim form is Nov. 16, 2026. If you’ve ever shopped on any of the CVS websites or mobile apps prior to July 27, 2026, you’re considered eligible to receive payment, but you must still submit a claim. 

			

More from CNET

According to the official settlement website, customers who submit a claim without documentation may receive up to $5, and those who submit a claim with valid documentation of belonging to the class may receive up to $10, but the amount may be reduced depending on the number of valid claims submitted. 

As is typical with class action lawsuits, potential class members may also opt out of the settlement. Opting out of the settlement will prevent payment, but will allow you to maintain your rights to directly sue the company yourself. The final date to opt out of the settlement is Nov. 1, 2026.

The final hearing is set to take place on Dec. 1, 2026, and if the court approves the settlement, payments will be issued 120 days after approval. Class members can be paid via check, PayPal, Venmo or Zelle.

title: OpenAI just upgraded ChatGPT Voice in three ways
snippet: Talking to ChatGPT is getting better in three ways starting today. OpenAI is rolling out a collection of improvements to how ChatGPT Voice mode works. more…
fullText:
Talking to ChatGPT is getting better in three ways starting today. OpenAI is rolling out a collection of improvements to how ChatGPT Voice mode works. 

GPT-6, ChatGPT Work, and plugins

First, ChatGPT Voice can now be powered by OpenAI’s three GPT-6 models. Astra, the most capable, has been out for a few weeks. Sol and Luna, the new medium and small intelligence models were upgraded to GPT-6 yesterday.

Next, OpenAI says that plugins now work with ChatGPT Voice. This includes integration like email, calendar, and Slack. This was a big disconnect for ChatGPT Voice users before, so it should be a highly welcome change.

Lastly, ChatGPT Voice now works with ChatGPT Work on the web and mobile. ChatGPT Work is OpenAI’s cloud-connected agentic system that works everywhere. It’s sort of like Codex on the desktop, but available in more places.

Back in July, OpenAI brought modern voice control to the ChatGPT desktop app. It’s great to see this focus on voice continue with today’s ChatGPT Voice-focused update.

fullText:
Andrew J. Hawkins

 

is transportation editor with 10+ years of experience who covers EVs, public transportation, and aviation. His work has appeared in The New York Daily News and City & State.

In a widely expected move, Volkswagen announced Monday that it will replace the recently retired ID.4 crossover with the upcoming ID.Tiguan. The decision is an acknowledgment by the German automaker that its more recognizable nameplates like Tiguan are likely an easier sell with consumers, especially when it comes to EVs.

When it lands in Europe in early 2027, the ID. Tiguan will join the ID.Polo and ID.Cross to round out Volkswagen’s new-and-improved electric lineup. VW also confirmed that the ID.Tiguan will come to the US, where the ID.4 was previously manufactured, “at a later date.” Design details remain under wraps, as the ID.Tiguan is being kept under camouflage for now.

1/7

First introduced in 2020, the ID.4 was intended to be VW’s push into mass-market EVs. But rather than go up against big sellers like Tesla’s Model Y, the automaker wanted to compete with high volume gas vehicles like the Toyota RAV4 and Honda CR-V. While it never fully dethroned those rivals, the ID.4 did have some success, selling 950,000 units since 2021. VW says it ranks “among the most successful battery-electric vehicle model series of Volkswagen AG.” VW ended production of the ID.4 at its Chattanooga factory in April 2026.

The electric Tiguan will retain much of what worked about the ID.4, while correcting some of its shortcomings, such as its frustrating lack of physical controls. VW plans on giving the ID.Tiguan the same interior look as its ID.3 NEO and ID.Polo, the latter of which is a surprise sales hit in the EU. That means we can expect buttons for all four windows, rather than just two, as well as physical controls for both the volume and climate settings. VW’s Android Automotive-based operating system will also be featured — which means we’ll probably see a Gemini-powered voice assistant.

Volkswagen didn’t say whether the ID.Tiguan will get the new Rivian-developed software and zonal architecture that is expected to make its debut on the low-cost ID.Every1 hatchback.

fullText:
This week saw the debut of Qualcomm’s latest Snapdragon chips and, with it, the usual onslaught of Tensor hate around Google’s Pixel phones. Personally, I don’t care about those, but new launches around Qualcomm’s event have shown off a lot of other specs I’d much rather see Pixel adopt.

9to5Google Weekender by Ben Schoon is a part of our free newsletter that also includes ‘Inbox,’ a twice-weekly roundup of key stories from around the web by Daniel Bader. Sign up here to get Weekender delivered to your inbox every Sunday along with ‘Inbox’ on Tuesday and Thursday. You can find past issues here.

Google’s Tensor chip in Pixel phones has been a hot-button issue for enthusiasts for the entire time Google has been working on the project. And, I get it. Tensor is objectively not as powerful as a flagship Snapdragon or MediaTek chip and, with Pixel phones getting more and more expensive, that’s hard to accept. Google has solved many of the biggest deficiencies, leading to fairly wide acceptance from the “average Joe” customer base that Google is aiming for in the first place, but every year the same conversation comes back up with a new Snapdragon chip – “I wish that was in my Pixel.”

Qualcomm’s Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 6 family – I’m choosing to not put “Extreme” into that word salad here – looks incredible, and MediaTek’s new Dimensity 9600 Pro is also going to be solid. It’s totally okay to be annoyed that Pixels don’t get the same raw horsepower.

	

But, for me at least, it’s everything else that I wish Google would get a bit more on board with.

This week’s new chip launches also saw the announcement of new phones using those chips and, man, it’s wild how much faster these other brands are progressing compared to market staples like Pixel and Galaxy. The Xiaomi 18 Pro and Oppo Find X10 look insane. 

Xiaomi 18 Pro series goes official with ‘privacy screen,’ 8,500 mAh battery, and Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6

Oppo Find X10 series goes official with triple 200MP cameras, 8,000 mAh battery

8,000+ mAh batteries, a plethora of 200MP cameras, that’s the sort of stuff I wish I was getting on my Pixel. Forget horsepower, give me battery life and camera sensors that look good even before the power of computational photography steps in. The Oppo Find X9 Ultra was a big wake-up for me in that regard, as it was the first phone in quite a while that made me want to ditch the Pixel from my phone lineup (and I’m sure our Inbox author Daniel Bader is greatly enjoying it after prying it from my “Techtember”-ed fingers).

Google, if you’re listening, the rest of the Android world is frankly killing it on the hardware front right now. The software is still so-so in my book, but the practical wins that come from these all-out builds are too great to ignore. So, Pixel 12 maybe? Thanks.

Googlebook is here – what do you think?

Following a tease earlier this year, Google took the wraps off of its Android-based Googlebook platform. Five laptops, deep smartphone integration, and prices starting at $899. I’m personally skeptical, but I’m very curious to hear what you think about the new initiative.

Next year’s Android chips are here

As mentioned earlier, Qualcomm and MediaTek both made big announcements this year, those being their respective new chipsets for Android flagships. Qualcomm has a pair of Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 6 chips, one more powerful than the other, while MediaTek has a Dimensity 9600 Pro alongside a variant designed for the “flagship killer” segment. Expect plenty more new Android phones to be announced in the coming weeks with these chips.

title: AT&T seemingly has no plans to support Apple’s new iPhone Handoff feature
snippet: Apple last week launched a new iPhone Handoff feature, which lets you use a single phone number across two iPhones. The number intelligently moves between each iPhone based on whichever one you pick up. iPhone Handoff requires support from cellular carriers, and it sounds like AT&T isn’t interested in adopting the feature. more…
fullText:
Apple last week launched a new iPhone Handoff feature, which lets you use a single phone number across two iPhones. The number intelligently moves between each iPhone based on whichever one you pick up.

iPhone Handoff requires support from cellular carriers, and it sounds like AT&T isn’t interested in adopting the feature.

Will AT&T support iPhone Handoff? 

As reported by CNET, AT&T seemingly has no plans to support iPhone Handoff. According to the report:

“While we see that there could be potential in capabilities like iPhone Handoff,” the spokesperson replied, “our focus remains on delivering innovations that make life simpler and keep customers connected with confidence.” They then pointed to “existing eSIM activation and transfer options across compatible devices.”

This will be frustrating news for AT&T subscribers. The carrier’s emphasis on “existing eSIM activation and transfer options” seemingly indicates it doesn’t have a complete grasp on how iPhone Handoff works, and why it’s significantly more seamless than manually moving an eSIM back and forth between two iPhone models.

I’ve been using iPhone Handoff for the last week while testing the iPhone 18 Pro lineup, and it really does feel like magic. As Apple promised, my number instantly switches to whichever iPhone I pick up.

It is a bummer that T-Mobile is charging $5 per month for iPhone Handoff, though it’s not necessarily surprising. It’s still significantly cheaper than having a second cellular plan altogether.

As of right now, T-Mobile is the only carrier in the United States to support iPhone Handoff. Apple says that Verizon will add support by the end of the year, “with more carriers to follow.” Outside the United States, Telekom Germany is a launch partner for the feature. Apple says EE will add support by the end of the year.

title: SpaceX preps next-gen Starlink as Amazon’s competitor stalls
snippet: SpaceX is gearing up for a monumental flight today that's sure to be closely watched by Amazon. If successful, SpaceX will deploy its first Starlink V3 satellites, which tout meaningful upgrades to the ever-expanding Starlink constellation. The 26 satellites will be riding atop Starship, which SpaceX will also attempt to deploy into Earth orbit for the first time. The mission arrives amid Amazon's ongoing setbacks with launch partners that are keeping its own Leo satellites grounded, and falling further behind its plan to offer a meaningful rival to Elon Musk's space internet service. It's been 12 weeks since Amazon's last successful Leo de … Read the full story at The Verge.
fullText:
Jess Weatherbed

 

is a news writer focused on creative industries, computing, and internet culture. Jess started her career at TechRadar, covering news and hardware reviews.

SpaceX is gearing up for a monumental flight today that’s sure to be closely watched by Amazon. If successful, SpaceX will deploy its first Starlink V3 satellites, which tout meaningful upgrades to the ever-expanding Starlink constellation. The 26 satellites will be riding atop Starship, which SpaceX will also attempt to deploy into Earth orbit for the first time. The mission arrives amid Amazon’s ongoing setbacks with launch partners that are keeping its own Leo satellites grounded, and falling further behind its plan to offer a meaningful rival to Elon Musk’s space internet service.

It’s been 12 weeks since Amazon’s last successful Leo deployment with 29 satellites carried into orbit aboard United Launch Alliance’s (ULA) Atlas V rocket on July 2nd. That brings Leo’s launched satellite total to 396 — far below the over 11,000 satellites that Starlink currently has in operation, or even the 552 Starlink satellites that have launched since July 2nd. Following its last launch, Amazon Leo launch systems director Melissa Wuerl said that the company had “a clear path to increase launch and deployment cadence,” but that evidently hasn’t happened.

Issues blighting Leo’s launch partners are largely to blame for the setbacks. Vulcan, ULA’s successor to the soon retiring Atlas V rocket that Amazon has relied on, has been grounded by the US Space Force since February 2026 following a booster anomaly that’s still under investigation. Blue Origin, the space company owned by Amazon founder Jeff Bezos, is similarly contracted to launch Leo satellites, but its New Glenn rocket has also been grounded since its only launchpad was destroyed in May.

Earlier this month, Amazon announced that it had ordered six additional launches for Arianespace’s A64 heavy lift rocket, bringing its total contracted launches from 18 to 24. This is also facing delays, however, following issues with an unspecified Ariane 6 component that’s expected to disrupt launches “for the remainder of 2026.” 36 Leo satellites were previously expected to launch aboard Ariane 64 in October, but those missions have since been scrubbed from the European spaceport website.

All of this begs the question: When will Amazon next expand its Leo constellation? The service is only in its early stages and has already received an extension for its FCC deadline to launch half of its planned 3,232 satellites, which came with the condition that the company needs to move quickly. Amazon previously said that the almost 400 satellites it has in operation are enough to switch on a limited version of its internet service, but the “mid-2026” deadline it set for commercial availability has passed with no update. At this rate, it’ll be years before Leo can seriously compete with Starlink globally.

title: Out of the Park Baseball lets me enjoy baseball even when the Mets suck
snippet: If you were to ask me what game or game series I've sunk the most time into, the answer would be easy: Out of the Park Baseball (OOTP). fullText:
If you were to ask me what game or game series I’ve sunk the most time into, the answer would be easy: Out of the Park Baseball (OOTP). I have spent roughly 2,300 hours, according to Steam, playing various editions of the game. OOTP isn’t like MLB The Show or Super Mega Baseball. It’s not graphically impressive. It’s not a blast of simple arcade fun. It is basically a spreadsheet pretending to be a video game. It’s fantasy baseball, but without having to wait six months to see how disappointing that sleeper draft pick will be, because you can plow through an entire season in as little as a few hours.

You can play individual games and dig into play-by-play managing in OOTP if you want. But that becomes tedious. And frankly, it’s not where the game is the most fun. Instead, I think the game is at its best when you sit in the GM’s chair and maybe make some helpful “suggestions” about how to structure the lineup or bullpen.

The UI is complicated and dense. 90 percent of the time, you’re just looking at rows of stats and scouting reports. And the level of detail is deep. OOTP includes not just current MLB players, but historical MLB players, all minor league teams, Korea’s KBO League, and even the entire World Baseball Classic.

There’s something thrilling about digging through all this info and trying to find that diamond in the rough during a draft. Someone who might become the new franchise player for your favorite team in this alternate universe. Deciding whether to bet on that prospect developing into a superstar, or to trade them for an undeniable big-league All-Star is stressful. And you even have to worry about fans abandoning you if you fail to re-sign their favorite player.

On my Mets, Brandon Nimmo isn’t just a good player, he’s a damned superstar. Kodai Senga has won three Cy Young Awards. I signed Juan Soto, but also traded a raft of mid-tier prospects for Ronald Acuña Jr., made the playoffs four years in a row, and eventually won a World Series. (Look, as a Mets fan, I need this fantasy world, don’t harsh my vibe.)

Perhaps the best part of OOTP Baseball, though, is that it kinda lets you play however you want. It’s deeply customizable. You can manually play every game if you want. Or you can speed-simulate entire seasons in a couple of hours. Want an easier experience where players don’t get hurt? Turn down or off injuries. Don’t want to worry about budgets? Play in commissioner mode and tell the team owner where to stick it. And because it mostly just sits there, statically waiting for you, it’s easy to just leave it running in the background and dip in and out when you’ve got a few spare minutes.

OOTP Baseball is a cozy sim for a very particular brand of sports nerd. If you love fantasy baseball and wish you could play it year-round (and don’t want to deal with friends arguing about whether their bid for Alonso came in on time), or maybe you dig the idea of a cozy game like Tiny Bookshop, but wish they had a more Sabermetric bent, OOTP Baseball might be for you.

The current version, OOTP Baseball 27, is available now on Steam or directly from the developer.

title: Apple says software update to fix iPhone 18 Pro rebooting bug is coming next week
snippet: On Monday, we reported on an issue where iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max users were seeing their phone freeze and reboot following a failed Face ID attempt. To us, it appeared to be a software glitch rather than an inherent hardware fault. Apple has now confirmed to 9to5Mac that a software update to address this problem is in the works, and should be available early next week. more…
fullText:
On Monday, we reported on an issue where iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max users were seeing their phone freeze and reboot following a failed Face ID attempt. To us, it appeared to be a software glitch rather than an inherent hardware fault.

Apple has now confirmed to 9to5Mac that a software update to address this problem is in the works, and should be available early next week.

Although the bug did not seemingly affect all users, it was reasonably widespread based on social media and 9to5Mac reader reports. 

At the time, we reproduced the problem on an iPhone 18 Pro device by obscuring our face with our hand as we attempted a Face ID authentication to access the Passwords app. The phone simply stops responding to touch input, and hard reboots after a few seconds. You could then find a panic log in the iPhone Analytics section of the Settings app.

iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max feature a redesigned Face ID sensor system, where the Infrared camera has moved behind the under the screen near where the clock is rendered in the status bar, resulting in a 25% smaller visible Dynamic Island. 

As we reported earlier in the week, some customers had already attempted to resolve the rebooting problem by swapping their phone with a new device at Apple, thinking it was a hardware fault. To reiterate, this is not necessary with a software fix now confirmed to be on the way. 

On a somewhat related note, Apple also just released watchOS 27.0.1 to fix a random restart issue with Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4.

title: MacBook Pro redesign is coming, with three features we’ve waited years for
snippet: Apple has a big MacBook Pro redesign in the works (possibly called MacBook Ultra) that’s expected to launch in October. Here are three rumored new features that we’ve waited a long time for. more…
fullText:
Apple has a big MacBook Pro redesign in the works (possibly called MacBook Ultra) that’s expected to launch in October. Here are three rumored new features that we’ve waited a long time for.

#1: OLED display

It’s hard to overstate the value of display technology for a product that many users spend all day looking at. Yet for years, the Mac has lagged behind Apple’s other products in offering the most cutting-edge display tech.

OLED has been a mainstay on iPhone for years, and iPad Pro introduced a tandem OLED in 2024 that many Mac users pined for. Now with the new MacBook Pro, OLED is finally coming to Mac.

The redesigned MacBook Pro with OLED is expected to offer truer blacks, improved contrast, and likely help out with battery life too. Here’s hoping it’s able to match the impressive tandem OLED the iPad offers.

#2: Touchscreen

Apple has long argued that the Mac doesn’t need a touchscreen, despite competing products nearly all offering touch. But rumors indicate we’re finally getting the first Mac with touch support.

The new MacBook Pro will have a touchscreen, and macOS 27 is already packed with hints that such a feature is coming. We’re expecting further software optimizations to make touch feel like a natural experience on the Mac.

Despite touch being available, macOS will remain tailored primarily for trackpad and keyboard input. Touch will be a secondary tool on the Mac, not replacing traditional input methods but rather supplementing them for users who have grown accustomed to touchscreens on iPhones, iPads, and PCs.

#3: No more notch

When Apple last redesigned the MacBook Pro in 2021, it introduced a notch design that first came to iPhone. The notch then spread to the MacBook Air too, making it a fixture of modern Mac design.

But the new MacBook Pro will reportedly drop the notch in favor of a hole-punch camera cutout that likely resembles what we’ve seen on iPhone Duo.

The Dynamic Island will be brought over to macOS too, making the camera cutout integrate seamlessly on the Mac like it does on iPhone. As someone who finds the notch more of an eyesore on the Mac than I ever did on iPhone, I’m excited to see the notch disappear soon.

title: ‘Brothers,’ starring Matthew McConaughey and Woody Harrelson, premieres on Apple TV
snippet: The first two episodes of “Brothers,” Apple TV’s new comedy series starring Woody Harrelson (Natural Born Killers) and Matthew McConaughey (Interstellar), are now available to subscribers. Watch the trailer below. more…
fullText:
The first two episodes of “Brothers,” Apple TV’s new comedy series starring Woody Harrelson (Natural Born Killers) and Matthew McConaughey (Interstellar), are now available to subscribers. Watch the trailer below.

’Brothers’ premieres on Apple TV

The “True Detective” co-stars are reuniting for “Brothers,” a new Apple TV series that riffs on the long-running rumor that Matthew McConaughey and Woody Harrelson may actually be half-brothers.

“Brothers” was announced last June, with Lee Eisenberg (The Office, Jury Duty) serving as showrunner, and both actors joining a long list of executive producers in addition to starring.

The show marks McConaughey’s second collaboration with Apple TV, following last year’s Apple Original Film “The Lost Bus.” For Harrelson, it is also his second project on the platform, following his role as Moe Berkus in “Fly Me to the Moon.”

This season of “Brothers” will consist of eight episodes, with new episodes premiering every Wednesday through November 4.

Here’s Apple TV on the show’s premise:

“Brothers” follows McConaughey and Harrelson, who play fictionalized versions of themselves, and whose lifelong friendship is thrown into chaos when they uncover a decades-old secret: they might actually be brothers. After Woody’s daughter’s wedding falls apart, he loads up the family and heads to Austin for an extended stay at Matthew’s ranch. But what begins as a healing getaway quickly spirals when Matthew’s mother, Ma Mac (played by Holland Taylor), accidentally lets slip a long-buried secret that the two friends might actually be brothers. As Woody turns the ranch upside down in pursuit of the truth, Matthew finds himself juggling an entirely different identity crisis: a potential run for Governor of Texas. The result is a heartfelt, chaotic and wildly funny story about friendship, family, fame and the messy line between myth and reality.

title: Apple and Qualcomm renew global patent licensing agreement
snippet: Qualcomm and Apple have renewed their global patent licensing agreement, extending a deal that was previously set to expire in 2027. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
Qualcomm and Apple have renewed their global patent licensing agreement, extending a deal that was previously set to expire in 2027. Here are the details.

Renewed deal takes effect next year

To say that Apple and Qualcomm have had a rocky relationship would be an understatement.

Once major business partners, the companies became embroiled in a sprawling legal battle in 2017 over Qualcomm’s patent licensing practices and royalty payments.

In a nutshell, Apple sued Qualcomm in U.S. federal court in early 2017, challenging Qualcomm’s patent-licensing practices and seeking nearly $1 billion in royalty rebates that Apple said Qualcomm had improperly withheld.

The lawsuit came just three days after the FTC also sued Qualcomm, alleging anticompetitive licensing practices. The complaint specifically mentioned Qualcomm’s dealings with Apple, alleging that the company offered billions of dollars in conditional rebates in exchange for Apple exclusively using Qualcomm modem chips in new iPhones and iPads.

A few months later, Qualcomm countersued Apple, accusing the company of breaching agreements and interfering with its relationships with iPhone and iPad manufacturers.

The dispute ended in 2019, when Apple and Qualcomm agreed to drop all litigation against each other worldwide.

As part of the settlement, Apple made an undisclosed payment to Qualcomm that, among other things, resolved a dispute over royalty payments Apple had withheld during the legal battle. The companies also entered into a six-year global patent licensing agreement and a separate multiyear chipset supply deal.

That licensing agreement took effect on April 1, 2019, and included an option for Apple to extend it for another two years. Apple ultimately exercised that option, extending the agreement through March 2027.

Today, Qualcomm announced that the companies have renewed the agreement once again, with the new deal taking effect on April 1, 2027.

The full press release read:

Qualcomm Incorporated today announced the renewal of its global patent license agreement with Apple, effective April 1, 2027.

“We are pleased to extend the Apple license agreement,” said John Han, Executive Vice President and General Manager of Qualcomm Technology Licensing (QTL).

The company did not disclose how long the renewed agreement will remain in effect, while Apple has yet to comment on the renewal.

It is worth noting that today’s announcement is unrelated to Apple’s use of Qualcomm modems on iPhones, something that has been widely discussed recently, as Apple used a Qualcomm modem in the U.S. version of the iPhone 18 Pro Max while relying on its own C2 modem elsewhere.

Apple has not officially commented on what its modem plans will look like going forward, but the expectation has been that the company will eventually move away from Qualcomm modems altogether.

snippet: Apple announced this week that creators will soon be able to offer video through Apple Podcasts Subscriptions, “including subscriber-exclusive episodes, ad-free video, early access, and bonus content.” Here are the details. more…
fullText:
Apple announced this week that creators will soon be able to offer video through Apple Podcasts Subscriptions, “including subscriber-exclusive episodes, ad-free video, early access, and bonus content.” Here are the details.

Apple Podcasts Subscriptions to get support for video

Back in 2021, Apple announced Apple Podcasts Subscriptions. This service lets creators offer paid subscriptions to their shows in exchange for perks such as ad-free listening, bonus episodes, early access, and subscriber-only content.

Since then, creators have been able to offer paid subscriptions through Apple Podcasts to listeners in more than 170 countries and regions.

With the podcast market increasingly shifting toward video, Apple has been expanding the format across its platform.

Earlier this year, Apple introduced a new HLS-based video podcast experience that lets users seamlessly switch between watching and listening, view episodes full-screen, download videos for offline viewing, and more.

More recently, with iOS 27 and its other software updates, Apple expanded video support in Apple Podcasts with features including read-along transcripts, chapters, media links, and playback on Mac and Apple TV.

Now, Apple has announced that video is coming to Apple Podcasts Subscriptions as well.

This means creators will be able to offer subscriber-exclusive video episodes, ad-free video, early access, and bonus video content through the same subscription system currently used for premium audio.

From Apple’s announcement:

Since Apple Podcasts Subscriptions launched, creators have built direct-to-listener businesses around premium audio. Adding video opens new opportunities for you to connect with your audiences and grow your business.

A new way to grow your business: Apple Podcasts Subscriptions already help creators build direct-to-listener businesses around premium audio. With the introduction of video, you have new ways to connect with audiences and expand your business directly on Apple Podcasts.

Streamlined delivery: Deliver both audio and video seamlessly without maintaining separate offerings or workflows.

A familiar Apple experience: Audiences can discover and enjoy premium video across Apple devices and the web, wherever and however they choose to tune in.

title: Google Maps update shows traffic lights and stop signs at your next turn on Android Auto, more
snippet: Google Maps is rolling out a new update on Android Auto that makes it easier to know what to expect at your next turn, with a visual indicator to show upcoming traffic lights or stop signs. more…
fullText:
Google Maps is rolling out a new update on Android Auto that makes it easier to know what to expect at your next turn, with a visual indicator to show upcoming traffic lights or stop signs.

It’s been around six years since Google Maps started showing traffic lights and stop signs along your route, but a new tweak gives these more relevance to your actual route. Where Maps previously showed these as fixed parts of the map, there’s a new pop-up that shows what to expect at upcoming intersections.

	

Alongside the floating name of the street at your next turn, Google Maps on Android Auto now also highlights whether you’ll see a traffic light or a stop sign at that intersection. We first observed this behavior earlier this week, and it’s been showing consistently in the time since. It’s also showing on the phone directly, which means iPhone users seeing the update will likely also see this on CarPlay.

It’s a subtle tweak, but it’s also a very glanceable way to give drivers a better idea of what to expect at a coming intersection, which could be invaluable if you’re driving around an unfamiliar area.

	

Like many visual updates, this is likely a server-side update for Google Maps. Let us know in the comments below if you’re seeing this update.

snippet: With Liquid Glass now a year old, Google apps on iOS are beginning to incorporate the translucent material alongside its Material 3 Expressive design language. more…
fullText:
With Liquid Glass now a year old, Google apps on iOS are beginning to incorporate the translucent material alongside its Material 3 Expressive design language.

Previously, the Google Photos floating bottom bar on iOS had a solid background, just like the Android version. As of version 7.94, it’s now made of Liquid Glass.

The screenshots on the left show the “Default” translucency level, while the “More clear” option is on the right and lets you see more of the image behind it. With the dark theme, you see how the default blue accent color tints the current tab indicator.

Google has also updated buttons in the top bar with Liquid Glass.

	

The traditional bottom bar in Google Health has also been updated with Liquid Glass. You can see what’s under the navigation element, while the “Ask Coach” FAB (floating action button) gets a frosted treatment.

The company is still in the process of phasing out the previous Google Material Theme design language on iOS with Material 3. Google Docs, Sheets, Slides, and Keep have been stragglers, while Tasks was updated fairly recently.

More broadly, Google has shown no interest in adding Dynamic Color to its iOS apps. It could add a manual system that lets users choose an accent color across all Google apps. That said, without system access to the wallpaper, it’s a bit pointless, with Dynamic Color always more of a system-level Android feature.

snippet: Apple has redesigned the Apple Pay checkout flow in iOS 27 for apps and websites. The changes make it easier to switch between different payment cards and see key details about the order you’re placing. more…
fullText:
Apple has redesigned the Apple Pay checkout flow in iOS 27 for apps and websites. The changes make it easier to switch between different payment cards and see key details about the order you’re placing.

In iOS 27, you can now swipe between payment cards right on the main Apple Pay interface. You can also tap a card to view a grid-style interface that shows all your available Apple Pay cards in one place.

The design allows them to seamlessly swipe to switch cards, conveniently surfacing important information about their eligible cards in Apple Wallet — including rewards, balances, debit account balance, pay later options, and more — so they can make more informed payment decisions.

Merchants and developers have control over what appears on the Apple Pay payment sheet, depending on the exact information they need to complete your order.

The iOS 26 version of the Apple Pay checkout flow has been criticized for being unintuitive. For instance, people often tapped the wrong thing when trying to switch between payment cards. The instinct is to tap the card itself, but in iOS 26, that would take you to the address-editing interface. You’d have to tap a separate button at the bottom to actually switch to a different card. iOS 27 streamlines all of this and makes it a lot clearer.

Bringing video and app split view to the iPad mini‘s display seems like a no brainer to me, especially given the fact that the iPhone Duo and iPad mini share similar aspect ratios. At least personally, I’d use an iPad mini in portrait a lot more if this feature existed.

title: You Might See Prime as a Shipping Option on Sites Other Than Amazon. How It Works
snippet: Some independent stores are now offering Prime delivery without you having to log in to your Amazon account.
fullText:
Free and fast delivery could be an option where you least expect it. More independent stores might be offering Amazon Prime shipping on their websites, and you won’t need to log into your Amazon account to get it.

The announcement this week is an expansion of the company’s Amazon Supply Chain Services, in which merchants pay the company to house their inventory and pick, pack and ship items to customers. Sellers will not have to pay extra to use Prime shipping as an option for customers and can keep their usual payment processing, order management and store policies.

So, imagine you’re shopping for items at one of the thousands of independent, non-Amazon.com stores on the internet. You select some things to buy, head to checkout and see Prime as one of the shipping options. That could mean fast and free, if you have a Prime account.

			

More from CNET

It’s not an entirely new thing — independent stores have offered Prime shipping on their websites before. What’s different now is that you won’t have to click on a “Buy with Prime” widget and then log in to your Prime account. You can finish checkout on the store’s website.

Read more: Amazon’s Early Prime Day Deals Are Here. Grab the Top Discounts Before They’re Gone

If you choose Prime as the shipping option, Amazon will confirm that you’re a member after the order is placed.

CNET reached out to Amazon to see if the company has a list of independent retailers offering Prime shipping, but a representative did not immediately respond.

There are more than 240 million Prime subscribers worldwide, 180 million of those in the US.

title: Apple’s 20th Anniversary iPhone 20 Pro May Arrive as a Seamless Slab of Glass
snippet: Next year’s models could have the biggest screens in iPhone history.
fullText:
Hope there’s extra room in your pockets. A new rumor says Apple’s iPhone 20 Pro and Pro Max could have the largest displays in iPhone history, alongside a quad-curved, nearly all-glass exterior.

Digital Chat Station, a prominent anonymous tech insider on the Chinese social media platform Weibo and a reliable source of Apple news in the past, posted over the weekend that the iPhone 20 Pro screen would be 6.41 inches and the Pro Max 6.96 inches, measured diagonally. The iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max, which hit stores last Friday, measure 6.27 inches and 6.86 inches (which Apple rounds up to 6.3 inches and 6.9 inches). The iPhone Duo, Apple’s long-awaited first foldable phone, which reaches stores on Oct. 23, has a diagonal 7.6-inch inner display when open.

A representative for Apple did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

			

More from CNET

CNET Senior Reporter Abrar Al-Heeti said that larger screens are great for watching videos and working on the go, but bigger displays also mean higher costs for consumers, serving as an “excuse for companies to charge you more.” 

“Along with the commemorative angle of the iPhone’s 20th anniversary, it’s likely Apple could use design elements like a bigger screen and an all-glass design to hike prices,” Al-Heeti said. 

More glass, smaller Dynamic Island

Digital Chat Station backed Bloomberg reporter Mark Gurman’s August report that the exterior of the new flagship phones would be nearly all glass in what’s called a quad-curved design. That means the glass will wrap around all four sides of the phone, making it look as if there is no bezel.

In his report last month, Gurman said that the glass on the front and back of the phones would “curve into the sides of the devices, with a metal band in the middle.”

The exteriors of the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max are made of aluminum and ceramic glass.

The iPhone 20 Pro and Pro Max will also have a smaller Dynamic Island and a tiny punch-hole selfie cutout on the front, according to Digital Chat Station.

The Dynamic Island is the capsule-shaped region at the top of the front screen that houses the selfie camera. It also expands and contracts to display notifications, system alerts and background activities.

The iPhone 20 Pro and Pro Max are expected to launch in September 2027 as the next iteration in the series. Apple is widely expected to skip over the iPhone 19 name and jump straight to iPhone 20 next year, marking the 20th anniversary of the first iPhone launch in 2007.

title: Ninja CrushBoss Review: The Perfect Blender If You Hate Chopping Vegetables
snippet: The food processor and blender attachments are handy, while other elements feel like overkill.
fullText:
Where to put it? That’s the question that stops many of us from buying another countertop appliance. In my small kitchen, every new piece of equipment means pushing another one out. Larger kitchens have more room to work with, but even they can end up more cluttered than one would like.

This modestly sized blender does far more than blend.  John Carlsen/CNET

Eventually, you need to decide if you’ll use an appliance often enough to justify getting it. In my case, I’m much more likely to choose a multipurpose product like an Instant Pot pressure cooker or an air fryer. Perhaps this is why I was excited to test out the Ninja CrushBoss, which combines a large blender, food processor and small smoothie blender into a single device. I spent the two weeks using a sample unit from Ninja in my kitchen, and I’m eager to share my thoughts. 

4 appliances in 1? Well, kind of

The main appeal of the Ninja CrushBoss is that it comes with three vessels: a 72-ounce blender pitcher, a 64-ounce food processor bowl and a 26-ounce smoothie tumbler.

CrushBoss isn’t Ninja’s first attempt at an all-in-one kitchen system, as the Ninja Detect, Ninja Professional Plus and Ninja Foodi Power Blender all attempt similar feats. What sets Ninja CrushBoss apart are the PrecisionDice and MultiBlade Disc attachments for the food processor bowl, plus a better smoothie tumbler design than previous models.

			

More from CNET

Similarly, the blender’s preset programs change depending on which vessel you attach to the 1,850-watt base motor, with each program running automatically to achieve the desired results. You can rotate the outer ring of the small LCD screen to choose your setting, then make the final selection by pressing the top of the screen inward. It’s not a touchscreen, but it’s easy enough to use once you learn the controls.

Intelligent blending features, PrepIQ and SmoothSense, track the type and consistency of what you’re blending, but I didn’t notice a difference compared to the preset programs or custom speed controls.John Carlsen/CNET

There isn’t much that’s special about the large blender pitcher, which uses largely the same design as other standalone Ninja blenders. It comes with a single blade assembly and presets for mincing, small chopping and large chopping. The smoothie tumbler is similarly simple, with its small blade assembly supporting ice crushing, blending and smoothie presets. Compared to older tumblers, the Travel Tumbler’s main upgrades are a better carrying handle, flip-top lid, and large smoothie straw — it’s more like a Stanley cup than a NutriBullet personal blender.

Last but not least is the food processor, which has the most accessories, including a chopping blade, dough blade, MultiBlade Disc, and the PrecisionDice assembly. Where the Ninja Detect’s food processor included reversible stainless steel discs, the MultiBlade attachment is largely plastic, with specific inserts depending on the model you choose. The model I tested came with inserts for thick slices, crinkle-cut slices and shredding — Ninja also sells inserts for thin slices, french fries and julienning.

While I understand that the plastic MultiBlade Disc and inserts reduce the amount of stainless steel in the package, I can’t help but wonder about their long-term durability compared to all-metal discs.John Carlsen/CNET

I call it a kind of four-in-one appliance because the smoothie tumbler’s main benefits are, naturally, smoother blending consistency than the large pitcher and greater travel portability with the included lid and smoothie straw. You can still use the large pitcher for family-size smoothies and anything too big for the other two vessels, so adding a blending function to each vessel is largely superfluous. Similarly, the dicing kit is hardly an appliance on its own, since you’ll see it on other food processor brands like KitchenAid and Breville.

How useful is the Ninja CrushBoss?

The point of the cheese test was to find the food processor’s limits, so I’m happy to report the motor safety cutoff and error messages worked as intended when I stressed the unit too much.John Carlsen/CNET

Of the three vessels, I spent the most time with the food processor. I used the PrecisionDice attachment to prepare a fruit salad, which went very smoothly and had no issues with mango, watermelon, strawberries and pineapple. I pureed some blackberries with the food processor’s chopping blade to add more texture to the salad, though the smoothie attachment was ultimately a better option for crushing the blackberry seeds.

Next, I swapped the dicing attachment for the MultiBlade and sliced potatoes and cucumbers with the normal and crinkle-cut attachments. Again, the results were very good. Things were a little less consistent when I processed carrots and cabbage with the shredder for a quick coleslaw, as some bits of each remained unprocessed between the blade and lid. The amount of unprocessed vegetables was minimal, so I tossed them into a bowl of ramen instead of chopping them by hand for the coleslaw.

To give the food processor a proper workout, I brought out the cheddar cheese and ran it through the shredder, slicer, and dicer. As you might suspect, the cheese worked best with the shredder, with very little waste and no clogs. The other two attachments are less suitable for cheese, with the slicing disc producing passable slices. However, I clogged the dicing tool when I tried to make cheese cubes. I ultimately succeeded with some tiny cubes, but I don’t recommend it. 

	

			

	

			

									

						Best Blenders We Tested in 2026					

							

		

While I didn’t use the dough blade attachment much, it seemed good for mixing bread dough into a state where I could knead it by hand. I ran three cycles using the dough preset — though I admit the last cycle was because I forgot to add an ingredient. One reason I finished by hand was that I could hear the motor straining a bit toward the end of the second and third cycles.

Even if I’m not 100% on board with using it for dense bread dough, the unit is plenty powerful for cookie dough and cake batter.John Carlsen/CNET

I suspect the CrushBoss can handle the job, as the manual says it can hold up to 2 pounds of dough and shut off if necessary, but it took only a minute of hand-kneading after processing to reach the consistency I wanted. My advice: Listen to your machine and avoid tasks that trigger the auto-shutoff too often. Fortunately, my testing didn’t surface any problems with the system’s durability.

Beyond the food processor bowl, little stood out about the blender pitcher and smoothie tumbler attachments. Each did well with various levels of blending, pureeing and ice crushing, but nothing so outstanding that my ancient Oster blender couldn’t also do. The biggest advantages over my modest blender are the pitcher’s size — even if it’s more than I need in my kitchen — and the tumbler’s portability. Ninja says CrushBoss isn’t suitable for hot blending, so you can’t safely use it with hot liquids.

The challenge of modular kitchen systems like Ninja CrushBoss

Somewhat paradoxically, the modular nature of the Ninja CrushBoss is also its biggest weakness — at least for me.John Carlsen/CNET

Although I’m happy that I don’t have to store three motorized bases for separate specialty appliances, all of Ninja’s vessels and attachments are bulky enough that they’d take up an entire shelf in my kitchen cabinets. There’s not really a safe way to store the extremely sharp food processor discs, so I ultimately kept them in a carrying case for a massage gun I threw out ages ago. Fortunately, you can safely store the largest blender blade assemblies in each vessel.

The other challenge is that while all of the attachments are dishwasher-safe, that only applies to the top rack. My older dishwasher’s top rack isn’t adjustable, so I can’t fit any of the vessels inside and I have to wash them all by hand. This isn’t a problem I experience with the glass jar of my Oster blender, or the slightly smaller vessel of the Tribest Backspin I tested in 2025. At least the other parts fit, which made cleanup much more manageable.

My point in calling these out isn’t to discourage anyone interested in the CrushBoss, but to note that storage space and dishwasher space still matter before you buy.

Should you buy the Ninja CrushBoss?

The CrushBoss’s value becomes more apparent as your food volume increases.John Carlsen/CNET

As I used the Ninja CrushBoss 4-in-1, I kept coming back to one central question: “Who is this for?” Ultimately, it’s a harder question to answer than I thought. I have no problem recommending each function separately — blending, smoothies, dicing and food processing — because it seems to do all of these well enough.

For example, this particular setup should work well for two types of households: large families and meal preppers. I grew up in a large family, and having an appliance to prepare a huge amount of ingredients for every meal is a no-brainer. Another group that might benefit is the meal-prepper, regardless of household size.

Still, selling everything together in a single kit is excessive for someone like me, who has a small apartment. I have plenty of travel cups for smoothies and rarely need to process large amounts of food. Ninja thankfully offers various CrushBoss configurations and will most likely sell the attachments separately down the line, like with its older products. Personally, I’d love a configuration with only a large pitcher and food processor — I don’t need a smoothie tumbler.

At $320, the Ninja CrushBoss 4-in-1 costs about what you’d pay for separate Ninja appliances, but it is pricier than previous generations of Ninja’s modular kitchen systems, even without the dicing kit. This is a drop in the bucket compared to getting similar attachments for a Vitamix Ascent X. Despite my personal reservations, I think the Ninja CrushBoss 4-in-1 is a great idea, especially for folks looking to consolidate multiple specialty appliances into a single modular system. It taps into the reason why people love the classic KitchenAid stand mixer, and that’s a good thing.

title: Apple Notes keeps getting better, here’s what’s new in iOS 27
snippet: iOS 27 adds new features for CarPlay, the Messages app, and a lot more, including a handful of Apple Notes upgrades. Here’s what’s new for Apple Notes in iOS 27. more…
fullText:
iOS 27 adds new features for CarPlay, the Messages app, and a lot more, including a handful of Apple Notes upgrades. Here’s what’s new for Apple Notes in iOS 27. 

Divider line added for organizing your notes

Joining the many different formatting tools already available in Apple Notes, iOS 27 lets you add divider lines to your notes.

It’s pretty simple. Just tap where you want the line to go, open the edit menu, and choose the new ‘Insert Divider Line’ option.

Divider lines are a great new way to organize content in a note, and a welcome addition to the Notes toolset.

Section links

Section links are now supported in iOS 27’s Notes app, letting you build a table of contents or other structure to navigate longer notes with ease.

To create a section link, select text inside your and open the edit menu. From there, hit ‘Add Link’ to see a new option: Link to Section.

This opens a menu where you’ll find all of the headings and subheadings currently found in your note. You can tap to select one, which will create a direct link to that section embedded in your text.

Create and add to notes with Siri AI

The single Notes upgrade I’m most excited about in iOS 27 involves Siri.

Apple’s new Siri AI lets you quickly, seamlessly add information to a new note or existing note in Apple Notes.

You can do this, for example, with any answer Siri provides in the new Siri app. Or you can do what I did (seen above) where I asked Siri to take a poorly formatted list and reformat it, then add it to a new note.

This works for existing notes too, just tell Siri which note you want to add to. Siri has offered some limited Notes capabilities in the past, but the new integration is a big upgrade.

Copy and paste Markdown

Last year in iOS 26, Apple Notes gained support for importing and exporting Markdown.

If you’re unfamiliar with Markdown, it’s a text formatting syntax created by John Gruber. With Markdown, you can write in plain text using special syntax for headings, links, lists, bold and italics formatting, and more. It’s a popular tool for writers who publish content online.

With iOS 27, Apple Notes is getting even more Markdown-friendly.

Now when you paste Markdown-formatted text into a note, it’s automatically converted into rich text. There are zero extra steps required. And if you want to copy text from your note as Markdown, there’s a new Copy as Markdown option you’ll find in the edit menu.

Image Playground upgrades

iOS 27 brings big upgrades to the Image Playground app and its underlying AI models. And since Image Playground is a key built-in feature of the Notes app, Notes users benefit too.

Per Apple’s press release:

Image Playground offers new powerful ways for users to bring their imagination to life. They can create high-quality images in virtually any style, now including photorealistic, thanks to a new generative model that runs on Private Cloud Compute. This is a major transformation for image generation across platforms. And generated images will automatically include a hidden SynthID watermark to identify them as AI-generated.

Apple Notes in iOS 27: wrap-up

Notes also features a variety of smaller UI refinements in iOS 27, including:

Newly refreshed app icon

Liquid Glass updates for buttons, menus, and more

Shared folder at top of folders list adds new icon

Individual shared folders and notes have updated icons too

title: The iPhone 18 Pro: The best and final iteration of the current form factor?
snippet: There’s a running joke that Apple always breathlessly announces that each year’s iPhone Pro is “the best iPhone we’ve ever made,” as if that were in some way surprising. But I do think that there’s some poignancy to the iPhone 18 Pro, because if the rumors about next year’s model are true, this could be the final iteration of the form factor that began with the iPhone X back in 2017. Specifically, we’re expecting next year to see the next big step toward that “single slab of glass” vision which will end the era of evolutionary change we’ve seen over the last decade … more…
fullText:
There’s a running joke that Apple always breathlessly announces that each year’s iPhone Pro is “the best iPhone we’ve ever made,” as if that were in some way surprising. But I do think that there’s some poignancy to the iPhone 18 Pro, because if the rumors about next year’s model are true, this could be the final iteration of the form factor that began with the iPhone X back in 2017.

Specifically, we’re expecting next year to see the next big step toward that “single slab of glass” vision which will end the era of evolutionary change we’ve seen over the last decade …

The evolution of the iPhone Pro models

If you were to line up every model from the iPhone 12 Pro to the iPhone 16 Pro, I think many people would struggle to tell the difference visually bar the switch from notch to Dynamic Island in 2022. The iPhone 17 Pro is still only an exception due to the extended camera island and Cosmic Orange option.

Of course, each model had new features, but I think even here it’s fair to say that unless a specific one has particular relevance to you personally, you really need to jump at least two or three generations before an upgrade amounts to a significantly better experience.

This in no way a criticism of Apple. The reality is that premium smartphones are a mature technology, at least in the conventional form-factor. We don’t see massive differences between successive generations because there’s only so much that can be done to improve them on an annual basis.

Apple is now experimenting with different form factors, starting with the iPhone Air and now, of course, the iPhone Duo – and we’re expecting another major design leap next year, in the form of a 20th anniversary model.

How exactly Apple will position next year’s design remains somewhat unclear. It was initially suggested that it would be a standalone model, distinct from the iPhone 19 Pro, while other reports suggest that it will be next year’s Pro model. There’s also the question of whether Apple will use sequential numbering or skip a number to mark the occasion, so it might instead be called the iPhone 20 Pro.

Personally, I do suspect that it will be the new iPhone Pro design, whether Apple calls it the 19 or 20. If this is correct, then the iPhone 18 Pro will be the final iteration of the form factor we’ve had for half a dozen years. 

I’m jumping two generations from the iPhone 16 Pro, so I’m going to separately list the new-to-me features introduced by each year’s models. I’m skipping improvements I see as trivial or completely irrelevant to my use, like 7-core GPU over 6-core and GenLock.

iPhone 17 Pro features carried forward

Center Stage front camera, for photos and video calls

Ultra-stabilised video

Dual capture

Telephoto lens up from 5x to 8x 

Telephoto sensor up from 12 MP to 48 MP

ProRes RAW video

Better battery life

Faster charging

New to iPhone 18 Pro

Wider maximum aperture on the main camera lens

Variable aperture main camera lens

Pro camera controls (aperture, shutter speed, white balance, histogram)

Photographic Styles v3

Smart focus tracking

Cinematic mode effects from standard video

Tap to zoom and rotate on the front camera

Smaller Dynamic Island, enabling three live activities

(Even) better battery life

(Even) faster charging

My personal … focus

Personally, there are five features I will be focusing on in my early usage.

Variable-aperture lens

While the headline feature is that variable aperture lens, I’ve said before that we probably shouldn’t expect too much from it. The maximum aperture is only marginally wider on such a small sensor, so I’m not expecting to see much difference in terms of shallow depth of field.

However, the maximum aperture does let in a little more light, amounting to around two-thirds of a stop. How much difference that will make remains to be seen, but it should translate to shorter Night Mode exposures. Since this is a feature I use a lot, often handheld, then I am looking forward to trying this.

Pro camera controls

The ability to control shutter speed will definitely have its uses for things like panning shots. And it will certainly be useful to be able to take full control of white balance. I’m also expecting the histogram to be useful when manually setting the exposure.

Photographic Styles v3

I’m generally not a filters kind of guy when it comes to either taking photos or editing them on the iPhone, preferring to do any editing using conventional adjustments afterwards. For that reason, I rarely used the existing Photographic Styles feature and don’t expect to make much use of the latest iteration either. But I must say I am intrigued by the film setting, so I’ll certainly be experimenting with this.

Smart focus tracking

One of the biggest weaknesses with autofocus when it comes to video occurs when the subject briefly passes behind something else and the camera can switch focus to the obstruction. Smart Focus Tracking claims to solve this problem, so I will certainly be putting this to the test.

Cinematic Mode effects from standard video

It’s less than a couple of months since I said that Apple appeared to have forgotten about Cinematic video mode. I said that was a great pity because, if Cinematic Mode video worked well, it would be an absolute game-changer for the practicality of the iPhone as a camera for more serious video work. So far, it has been frustratingly close but no cigar.

However, it appears I was wrong: one of the new iPhone 18 features is that the cinematic video effects can be applied to videos shot in standard mode.

It’s certainly very handy that we no longer need to decide in advance whether or not to use the mode, but what most interests me is that Apple is again paying attention to the feature. This suggests that it is indeed being shown some love, and we therefore can expect it to continue to improve in much the way Portrait mode did for still photos. I’m very much looking forward to testing this.

These, then, are the features I think could potentially make the most difference to me. How about you? If you’ve upgraded to the iPhone 18 Pro, what features drove your decision? Please share in the comments.

title: Square now integrates with Apple Business to improve Maps listings
snippet: Square has announced a new integration with Apple Business that should make Apple Maps better for both businesses and users. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
Square has announced a new integration with Apple Business that should make Apple Maps better for both businesses and users. Here are the details.

Square integration lets businesses easily keep Apple Maps listings up to date with accurate info

Have you ever been frustrated to learn that an Apple Maps business listing has outdated info? Maybe the listed hours are inaccurate, or it has an error in the address, phone number, and so on.

Square’s new integration with Apple Business should help. From the announcement:

Square today announced a new integration with Apple that enables Square sellers to connect their locations to Apple Business from their Square Dashboard, so they can seamlessly manage and synchronize key business location information that appears on Apple Maps. Rather than managing multiple channels separately, sellers can now maintain their Apple presence alongside the rest of their business in Square. The integration makes it easier for sellers to ensure Apple users see up-to-date and accurate information across Apple Maps, Siri AI, Apple Wallet and other Apple apps.

Per Square, this integration provides several key benefits to business owners. It lets them:

Manage their brand and add a logo across connected locations, allowing them to enhance and extend their brand presence to Apple Maps place cards, directly from Square Dashboard.

Automatically sync key business details for each connected location, such as hours, address, and phone number, so this information stays up-to-date and accurate across Apple Maps, Siri AI, Apple Wallet, and other Apple apps and services without manual updates.

Turn discovery into engagement across connected locations with action links such as Menu, Order, Pickup, Delivery, Book, or Schedule Appointment, so customers can take action directly from an Apple Maps place card.

The partnership sounds like a clear win for businesses, since so many already rely on Square. But it should result in a better Apple Maps experience for users over time too.

Business owners can learn more about the Square and Apple Business integration at squareup.com/partnerships/applebusiness.

snippet: The new iPhone 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max have been out for a week, and they have been amazing devices to use and test.
