title: Big Pixel VIPs widget redesign starts rolling out
snippet: Following the version 2.0 update rolling out earlier this week, Google is now beginning to launch the Pixel VIPs widget redesign announced in the September Feature Drop. more…
fullText:
Following the version 2.0 update rolling out earlier this week, Google is now beginning to launch the Pixel VIPs widget redesign announced in the September Feature Drop.

Previously, the widget could be expanded to take up your entire screen. This redesign limits Pixel VIPs to two layouts.

The 5×1 layout shows just one row of your prioritized contacts (up to four) at a time with the ability to scroll for more. This view pairs circular profile avatars with just first names, rather than including surnames as before. The change results in a more consistent widget appearance.

Old vs. new

	

The 5×2 configuration is now the max size for the Pixel VIPs widget. Depending on the number of contacts, Google will display rectangular cards that feature pill-shaped buttons to quickly call or message.

Meanwhile, unread messages will result in a circular badge appearing in the top-right of the circular profile or the messaging icon, which would benefit from being a little bit more noticeable in the latter configuration.

This is rolling out via a server-side update that is not yet widely available. It’s only appearing on one of our Pixel devices today.

title: Bellroy’s leather Pixel 11 Pro case is a keeper
snippet: Like any sane capitalist, I love getting new stuff. But there’s something heartening about those new things settling into age, like a fecund garden becoming slightly unwieldy, or a pair of shoes getting more comfortable as you use them. Similarly, I’ve always enjoyed the way a well-made leather case ages as it weathers the trials and tribulations of everyday life. Traditionally called a patina, it’s the lived-in quality that a piece of leather inherits as it absorbs skin oils, scratches, and the unpredictability of weather. more…
fullText:
Like any sane capitalist, I love getting new stuff. But there’s something heartening about those new things settling into age, like a fecund garden becoming slightly unwieldy, or a pair of shoes getting more comfortable as you use them.

Similarly, I’ve always enjoyed the way a well-made leather case ages as it weathers the trials and tribulations of everyday life. Traditionally called a patina, it’s the lived-in quality that a piece of leather inherits as it absorbs skin oils, scratches, and the unpredictability of weather.

So it was when I put on the new “Red Ochre” variant of the leather Pixel 11 Pro XL case from Bellroy. The Melbourne-based company has long been an official Made by Google partner, which means it’s always among the first case manufacturers to unveil its wares each August.

I’ve had the case on my phone for just over three weeks now, and I look forward to picking it up each time. Bellroy’s leather is thin and rigid, and is treated to prevent wear, which means that it takes longer than, say, a piece of Horween leather from Nomad, to age. But it also means it will look new for longer. Barring a few minor scratches, the case has survived more than a few child-related drops with aplomb.

	

On the structure side, the leather is reinforced with a rigid plastic frame that protrudes a millimeter or so above the display, and is covered internally by a microfiber lining. Magnets are present on the back for PixelSnap compatibility, and the buttons are made from anodized aluminum, which gives them a satisfying tactility akin to the phone’s buttons themselves.

At $59, this is not a cheap case, but to my eyes it’s the right combination of form and function. I love the color, though there are three others available — Black, Artichoke, and Pewter — if the more traditional saddle color is a bit too bright.

My weakness is a great leather case for any phone, but unlike iPhone and Galaxy cases there aren’t many good Pixel options. There’s this $40 option made by Snakehive that I plan to pick up, but it lacks coverage on the top, bottom, and right button side, which I dislike. Still, it appears to have more supple leather than Bellroy’s, which should patina more quickly, so I’m looking forward to putting them head-to-head in the future.

Until then, I’m quite happy with Bellroy’s leather Pixel 11 Pro XL case, and plan to keep it on my phone until something else newer, shinier, and patina-ier comes along.

title: The Googlebook has an opportunity to build Android like nothing else [Video]
snippet: Despite having effectively zero market share right now, there is an opportunity for Googlebook to do something that basically nobody else could do, but can they do it? more…
fullText:
Despite having effectively zero market share right now, there is an opportunity for Googlebook to do something that basically nobody else could do, but can they do it?

I’ll state right up top that I’m already cautiously optimistic. We need a competitor player to Mac and, in particular, Windows. Microsoft, as of late, has been nothing but combative with the people who use the firm’s operating system every single day. A new player is needed. I’m still not fully convinced yet by Googlebooks, but there is an opportunity, a big opportunity that hinges on quite a few things falling into place.

Considering how many new products are released every year, it’s quite surprising how few operating systems are unveiled. I suppose there is a caveat that Android has existed for a long time, but there have been no true attempts to make it work as a “proper desktop” experience, save Samsung’s DeX system, which was an internal attempt to make it work with Galaxy phones and tablets.

For more video content, subscribe to 9to5Google on YouTube.

	

DeX is a fine take on things, but it is limited by virtue of being an experience trying to emulate a desktop experience. Googlebook OS is Android reimagined for the desktop era.

I’m still not sure if this is too late or if there is enough interest. Google’s move comes at a very interesting time. Maybe its impending launch was the reason that Chrome OS has languished in recent years, having had lots of early promise and a surging user base, particularly in the education sector.

I have had the benefit of trying out Googlebooks, but in the lead-up to launch, I’ve been thinking more broadly about why now, and whether there is any real, tangible reason that Google would fully adopt Android across phones, tablets, and, now, desktops/laptops.

Bear with me, though, as a lot of assumptions have to be made for my points to fully hit home. I know that isn’t ideal, but just indulge me in this thought exercise at the very least.

The high-end might not be the ‘tip of the spear’

We’ve just seen a slew of expensive hardware unveiled under the Googlebook branding. These are the “optimum” hardware experiences, and I do think many are overpriced. That’s not where I see the benefits.

Compared to previous Chrome OS versions, Android devices are better optimized for low-power, low-resource use. A bad Chromebook is almost always worse than a bad Android device, at least in my experience. It’s harder to hide bad performance on a laptop or desktop because you’re used to certain power thresholds. On a tablet or phone, that isn’t as pronounced because things are almost always more lightweight.

It helps that many Android SoCs are powerful enough now to rival mid-range desktop processors or at least those found in notebooks.

Android seems to scale much better now than a few years ago, but as Apple has shown recently, you can run desktop-level applications on mobile SoCs. I could easily see a laptop running absolutely fine with a Snapdragon 8 Gen 3 from a few years ago and doing so with very low power consumption.

Just a few years ago, when Google Stadia was still around, the idea of a “gaming Chromebook” felt silly and wasteful. Those machines relied entirely on the cloud, meaning you were paying a premium for a laptop that couldn’t actually play games without perfect Wi-Fi. However, if we get gaming Googlebooks these could be a very different prospect. 

Hardware has evolved to the point where modern mobile processors easily outperform last-generation consoles like the PlayStation 4, bringing entry-level gaming power straight into a laptop chassis without needing an internet connection.

At the same time, the software side has improved drastically. Android gaming is no longer just for casual mobile apps; it now features massive, high-fidelity games that look and feel like console titles. Combined with the ability to emulate older PC and console games locally, a gaming Googlebook becomes a genuine, self-sufficient gaming machine you can actually take anywhere, and one that doesn’t require a wall outlet to play for hours at a time.

Unlike Steam Machines and the Steam Deck, Fortnite is there right from day one.

Something else to consider that I think has been glossed over by basically anyone, because we’re so accustomed to mouse and keyboard interactions with a laptop or desktop.

No other desktop-level operating systems have been developed from the ground up with touch interactions in mind. This is one of the other major USPs for Googlebooks; I’ve already said it multiple times in this rundown that Android only needs to close an application gap. That is exponentially easier than trying to shoehorn a legacy OS into a new form factor.

Apple has kept iOS, iPadOS, and MacOS all as separate OS builds. Google’s “everything is Android” approach could be a masterstroke. I’m resting heavy emphasis on “could” in that equation.

Why? Well, there is a generation of people out there who have grown up effectively “mobile first.” Kids who are now young adults, the “iPad kids” that are now getting to a stage where they are looking for a product that is familiar, comfortable, and does everything they need.

They’ve grown up already using tools like Capcut rather than Adobe. Playing mobile games or mobile ports of the biggest games, like Roblox. Traditional desktop paradigms have never catered to those young people. Googlebooks and the Android experience, rightly or wrongly, extend the familiar to a new form factor. It’s a play that I haven’t seen many discuss, but that could work if the price is right.

‘Desktop-level’ could bring even wider benefits

For the older folks, we have a bee in our bonnets about “desktop-level software”. It’s still essential that we get some things ported over sooner rather than later.

If, for instance, Blackmagic or Adobe port over their respective software packages, Davicini Resolve or Creative Cloud apps to Googlebook, that’s great. 

There’s a hidden secondary benefit, though. The next wave of foldable phones with potential support for desktop apps or desktop app scaling now have access to professional-grade applications in a form factor that is multiple times more portable than a traditional laptop. This extends to tablets, too.

I’m quite bullish that Android tablets could be one of the biggest beneficiaries with the introduction of the Googlebook, that is, if the company is willing to allow more power tools to come to the other versions of Android that the Googlebook OS is based on.

You can rebuke much of what I have said for any number of reasons, but everyone can agree that so much hinges on which brands are willing to start building for Android. Closing this “app gap” is arguably the most important component of the Googlebook during its first year.

I’m cautiously optimistic about the Googlebook program. A fully flexible, malleable operating system that spans regular smartphones, foldables, tablets, laptops, and potentially desktops could do something no other OS has offered before. Scalable in ways that not even Apple has been able to do, but has half-stepped toward since making iPadOS a midway experience or bridge between iOS and Mac.

If Google invests in and enhances Android across the entire stack, every existing and future device will evolve at a rate that wasn’t possible before. Scalable for any screen size. Apps that can be desktop-level while still being mobile native.

There is a big “if” here, and that is the only reason I’m not fully invested yet. The current, glaring software gaps need to be plugged – and plugged fast.

There is a parallel that might prove to be a good omen. Linux has had a massive swell of users over the past year, driven by Valve and, in particular, Steam OS. The success of the Steam Deck has proven that an alternative to Windows can work for gamers.

I’m not sure if we’ll ever get a compatibility layer in Android for various Windows or Linux applications, but who knows. It is not out of the realm of possibility, and if it happens, it’s going to be a major turning point. Google just has to be sure that this is a long-term project, and improving on Chrome OS is a must.

Proton has done wonders for Valve over the past 3 or 4 years. This is a blueprint Google could follow. I do think getting native ports for a few of the biggest applications is all it will take to get more on board. A small swell could quite easily become a bigger wave of app conversion.

A few years ago, if you’d asked me if my gaming PC would ever run an OS other than Windows, I’d have said “never”. I sit here 18 months after ditching it in favor of Linux’s performance gains.

That experience has taught me to be less dismissive of Android on desktop than I was some months ago, and my time playing with the first run of Googlebooks has me excited for what might be coming next for Android.

iOS 27 introduced Dual Capture support for FaceTime, letting you show your front and rear camera views at the same time. And in iOS 27.2, that upgrade is expanding to now support Group FaceTime calls.

Group FaceTime calls support Dual Capture in iOS 27.2 on compatible iPhones

FaceTime is a popular iPhone feature that, at its core, hasn’t changed much since first coming on the scene many years ago.

But iOS 27 introduced the first substantial upgrade in a while: Dual Capture support.

With Dual Capture, you can have your front and rear camera views active at the same time during your FaceTime call. Just hit the ‘Flip’ button on the viewfinder and whoever you’re talking to will see both of your camera views simultaneously.

Note: Dual Capture requires an iPhone 17 or later, and participants in the call need to be running iOS 27, iPadOS 27, or macOS 27 to see the dual camera streams.

iOS 27.2 is currently in beta, but it comes with a great upgrade for Dual Capture: Group FaceTime calls are now supported too.

In iOS 27.0, you can only use the feature in one-on-one calls. But if you join the iOS 27.2 beta, or just wait a few weeks for the public launch, you’ll get Dual Capture for all of your Group FaceTime calls as well.

title: OpenAI accuses Apple of improperly adding new evidence to trade secrets case
snippet: OpenAI and the other defendants in Apple’s trade secret misappropriation lawsuit made a new filing, asking the court to strike two expert declarations and disregard other evidence Apple recently submitted. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
OpenAI and the other defendants in Apple’s trade secret misappropriation lawsuit made a new filing, asking the court to strike two expert declarations and disregard other evidence Apple recently submitted. Here are the details.

A bit of context

As frequent 9to5Mac readers probably know, Apple recently filed a trade secret theft lawsuit against OpenAI, Jony Ive’s io Products, and two former employees: Chang Liu and Tang Tan.

In a nutshell, Apple is accusing its former employees of taking or accessing confidential hardware information after leaving the company and using it to benefit OpenAI’s consumer hardware efforts.

Apple has specifically alleged that Chang Liu accessed confidential engineering files after leaving Apple, while alleging that Tang Tan sought confidential information from Apple employees interviewing for jobs.

As part of the lawsuit, Apple has asked the court to issue a preliminary injunction barring OpenAI and the other defendants from accessing, using, disclosing, or soliciting Apple’s confidential information and trade secrets.

According to Apple, the injunction would prevent its trade secrets from becoming further embedded in OpenAI’s hardware development while the case plays out.

Apple files new evidence, OpenAI shoots back

As part of the legal back-and-forth over its motion for this preliminary injunction, Apple last week filed a reply brief supported by five expert declarations totaling 126 pages, along with 13 exhibits. The experts were Daniel Roffman, James Pooley, Dr. Ayman Fayed, Dr. Paul Hatch, and Dr. Jude Runge.

In these documents, Apple argued that OpenAI’s opposition failed to undermine its trade secret claims, and pointed to additional evidence that it says supports its allegations against Liu, Tan, OpenAI, and io Products.

The expert declarations, meanwhile, addressed and further detailed issues such as Apple’s security practices, forensic evidence from Liu’s devices, the value of its power-management trade secrets, and the secrecy of its metal-finishing processes, two key categories at issue in the lawsuit.

Now, OpenAI and the other defendants are shooting back, accusing Apple of improperly using its reply brief to introduce new evidence and expert opinions, including material they say could have been presented earlier, leaving the defendants without a fair opportunity to respond.

From the fling:

Apple submitted with its reply brief five new expert declarations (including one entirely new expert), totaling 126 pages, as well as numerous new exhibits. These declarations go far outside the scope of Apple’s opening brief and Defendants’ opposition, and in any event do not save Apple’s deficient motion.

The defendants also go through the new expert declarations in detail, arguing that Apple is effectively trying to shore up its original motion with new material after seeing the defendants’ response.

Among other things, they argue that Runge was brought in as an entirely new expert to reinforce testimony Apple had already submitted, and that Fayed offered new opinions that could have been included earlier.

They add that Pooley relied on an investigation conducted only after Apple filed its original motion, and that Roffman introduced evidence they say was available to Apple before that filing, while also presenting some of Liu’s communications out of context.

As a result, the defendants are asking the court to strike two of the new declarations, including Roffman’s five exhibits, and disregard other evidence and opinions that they say were improperly introduced.

Interestingly, they ask that if the court decides to consider Roffman’s declaration and exhibits anyway, it also take into account a new declaration Liu filed, offering his own explanation of the messages and device activity that Apple cited as evidence against him.

9to5Mac is brought to you by CleanMyMac by MacPaw. With the release of macOS 27 Golden Gate, use CleanMyMac first to free up space, optimize your system, and ensure your new Mac runs at 100% on day one. Learn more.

macOS 27 Golden Gate is a huge upgrade over macOS 26 Tahoe, and not just because of the smarter design decisions. Just like iOS 27 for iPhone, the Mac adds a Liquid Glass appearance slider. This lets you dramatically change the look of your Mac across the system.

The slider

Liquid Glass is Apple’s design language that started with iOS 26 and macOS 26 Tahoe. Initially, Liquid Glass started with a single look. Apple later added a setting to make Liquid Glass less clear.

Starting with iOS 27 and macOS 27 Golden Gate, Liquid Glass is no longer limited to just two styles. Instead, Apple has introduced an appearance slider. This lets you make Liquid Glass much more clear than before. You can also give Liquid Glass a more opaque look that still looks modern.

macOS 27 Golden Gate defaults to a medium setting. The system also invites you to adjust the slider during initial setup. You can also adjust the slider later in System Settings > Appearance.

The Liquid Glass slider provides a live preview of what to expect from each setting. Three notches suggest most clear, medium, and most opaque. However, you can assign it to any level in between notches as well.

The Dock

The Dock is the most prominent component that changes appearance based on the Liquid Glass slider setting.

It can range from showing your desktop wallpaper in clear definition to being a more opaque and defined material.

Here’s a closer look:

macOS desktop widgets can be full color, dim, or change automatically. The Liquid Glass slider changes how the dim widget appearance looks as well.

Apple Music and Podcasts

Apps like Apple Music and Podcasts that have system Now Playing bars have a very different look based on the Liquid Glass slider position.

Here’s the Now Playing bar Podcasts, for example:

And here’s Music: 

More

The slider also applies to sidebars, toolbars, and toolbar buttons. This changes the look of Photos, Safari, and other apps with window chrome.

The one thing about the Liquid Glass slider in macOS 27 Golden Gate is that a single slider controls all Liquid Glass appearances across the system. That means you get one look for the Dock, widgets, and window chrome. 

What’s your preference? More clear, more opaque, or somewhere in the middle? Personally, I really love how nice and mature the more opaque option looks on my Mac. Still, it can be fun to experiment with more clear, and I’m glad macOS 27 Golden Gate gives everyone the option to decide.

Share your thoughts in the comments!

title: Nest Doorbell has been triggering Gemini’s American accent, no matter what language you speak; fix coming
snippet: Google Home is experiencing a unique bug that announces Nest Doorbell notifications in an American accent, even if your preferences are set to literally any other language/dialect. more…
fullText:
Google Home is experiencing a unique bug that announces Nest Doorbell notifications in an American accent, even if your preferences are set to literally any other language/dialect.

According to one user on Reddit, Gemini has been responding to them in American accent only when its referencing their Nest Doorbell. That’s nothing out of the ordinary on the surface, but this user’s complaint revolves entirely around the fact that they’re French, speak French, and live in France. Even still, the Nest Doorbell seems to trigger Gemini’s US English.

It isn’t just affecting one user, or one device. A commenter expressed the same concern in the Netherlands, and another in the UK. For the user in the Netherlands, their Bosch washing machine alerts default to US English instead of Dutch. It sounds like every other interaction with Gemini happens in the language of choice, but certain appliances bring out a different Gemini voice altogether.

According to a response by an official Google account, the issue is being worked on. No fix has been rolled out, but Gemini will likely stop responding in its American accent soon enough, unless you specifically want that.

	

It might have been be a bug developed after the September Google Home update with changes to Gemini for Home. Spoken notifications seem to work as intended, but for whatever reason, Gemini chooses to give the user context in an American accent instead of the language or accent set in preferences. the only change note that refers to Gemini is one that improves follow up question behavior. Beyond that, there’s nothing pointing towards an obvious cause.

Something is clearly broken along the pipeline of information, but it’s manifesting in one of the most hilarious ways.

It’s a strange one, but Google is aware of the issue and claims to be working on it.

title: Apple retires the Apple Park Visitor Center’s unique AR experience
snippet: Earlier this summer, Apple closed a portion of the Apple Park Visitor Center as it worked to “improve our store.” That space has now reopened, and the big change is that Apple has removed the augmented reality experience that let visitors use custom iPads to view Apple Park. more…
fullText:
Earlier this summer, Apple closed a portion of the Apple Park Visitor Center as it worked to “improve our store.”

That space has now reopened, and the big change is that Apple has removed the augmented reality experience that let visitors use custom iPads to view Apple Park.

When Apple opened the Apple Park Visitor Center to the public in 2017, here’s how the company touted the AR experience:

Inviting guests to explore Apple Park in an immersive and engaging way, a 3-D model of the campus is brought to life by augmented reality technology.

Visitors can learn about the world’s largest naturally ventilated building and view one of the largest on-site solar energy installations in the world. Visitors can also choose to lift the entire roof off the building to peek inside to the collaborative office pod layout.

Until this change, the Apple Park Visitor was divided into three sections: the AR exhibit, a traditional-style Apple Store, and a cafe.

Source: RedNote

Now, Apple has retired the AR exhibit and transformed that space into an extension of the more traditional Apple Store. As spotted by MacRumors, this includes Avenues along the wall showcasing accessories and redesigned display tables featuring Apple products.

The rest of the Apple Park Visitor Center, including the cafe, remains unchanged.

9to5Mac’s Take

The AR experience at the Apple Park Visitor Center was unique, but after nine years it was starting to feel like that space could be better utilized in other ways. 

I wish Apple had tried something other than converting it into a traditional retail store, but at least the cafe remains as a unique fixture of the Apple Park Visitor Center.

title: Apple Photos in iOS 27 gets camera roll feature it’s long needed
snippet: iOS 27 is a big update for Apple’s Photos app, with improvements to slideshows, shared albums, and more. It also adds a welcome camera roll-type feature many have long been asking for: ‘Captured by Me.’ more…
fullText:
iOS 27 is a big update for Apple’s Photos app, with improvements to slideshows, shared albums, and more. It also adds a welcome camera roll-type feature many have long been asking for: ‘Captured by Me.’

‘Captured by Me’ in iOS 27 Photos app contains only photos and videos you shot in Camera app

Apple’s Photos app has steadily expanded its feature set over the years. In addition to being home to the photos and videos your iPhone captures, it also includes content that’s been shared with you, Memories, screenshots, saved media, and a lot more.

The Photos app used to offer a ‘Camera Roll’ feature that was similar to what the ‘Recents’ album does today. It included images you captured as well as ones you saved.

But what’s been missing for a long time is a feature that actually just shows photos and videos that you’ve taken—in other words, something that could more accurately be called your ‘camera roll.’

iOS 27 delivers that long-missing feature, and it’s called ‘Captured by Me.’

‘Captured by Me’ in iOS 27 is a new Photos collection that does exactly what it sounds like. It includes only media that’s been captured by your Camera app.

So photos and videos that you shot on your iPhone are collected there. But you won’t see screenshots, images your friends sent you, or any other types of content.

In addition to the dedicated ‘Captured by Me’ collection, you can also use a ‘Captured by Me’ filter in your main Photos library.

Whichever way you use the feature, ‘Captured by Me’ in iOS 27 fills an important gap in Apple Photos’ feature set.

title: What I learned after 30 days with the Pixel 11 [Video]
snippet: It has been almost 30 days since Google officially launched the Pixel 11 lineup, and the 11 might be the most sensible device of the bunch. Here’s what I have learned, having used it for the full month post-launch. more…
fullText:
It has been almost 30 days since Google officially launched the Pixel 11 lineup, and the 11 might be the most sensible device of the bunch. Here’s what I have learned, having used it for the full month post-launch.

For more video content, subscribe to 9to5Google on YouTube.

Less nip, more tuck

It’s hard to be annoyed too much about the Pixel 11 design, but I can 100% get a little bored. When you get a new phone, you may subconsciously want at least a few changes to help it feel “different.”

However, if you’ve not used the Pixel 9 or Pixel 10, you probably won’t even care. I know I’m not in the minority in loving the Pixel design, but there’s certainly a feeling of Groundhog Day after a while. What I’ve realized is that, as someone who has used the last three generations, to me, a case has felt more important than ever.

	

After a month of use, the flatter camera visor is one of the few “big” changes that feels more consequential. My dream would be a boxier shape akin to the Pixel 10a, but with a case on the phone, you can achieve that, or close to it.

A tangible change I hadn’t expected was the NFC chip moving closer to the top edge. In tandem with the smaller camera protrusion, I’m not clashing my phone against terminals or turnstiles, plus wireless payments are a lot faster, or at least feel more accurate.

I’m so glad we have stronger Pixelsnap magnets because you’re confident an accessory will stick, which is especially important because the slippery, glossy finish on the back glass was problematic with the Pixel 10 at times. I do wish that the phone didn’t sound so hollow to the tap, for a $900 phone, it can feel a little cheap, even though it has a great frame and mass. Little nitpicks, but I do care about extra attention in these areas. Maybe next year it’s time to address these admittedly minor build complaints.

As far as the design is concerned, the Pixel 11 builds on what was good; the good news is that there is very little bad. I hoped that we would get display brightness changes, but maybe it’s the endgame for this specific size and shape. I’m very unsure how Google will make major changes next year if we do get a proposed redesign. The only way I can see changes is in the materials used, some dimension shavings, but little else that can really refine the post-Pixel 9 formula. 

Does Gemini Intelligence matter?

I mean this in the most positive way possible. The Pixel 11 is more of the same, yet there are a few things that start to feel like they haven’t become game-changing in the ways that Google seems to expect. I’m not actively using many of the new functions that the Pixel 11 shipped with. I say “actively” as the hands-off background automation approach is what Google should excel at and isn’t quite doing so everywhere yet.

Proactive Assistance is on the cusp of being a truly exceptional upgrade for Magic Cue. I’m in the UK, so Google Messages is an app that I love, but don’t use with many contacts. I say this because when I’ve had suggestions for things like my passport number or my flight number on a trip, the instantaneous pop-up suggestions seem so perfectly integrated that it feels like Magic Cue on steroids.

We desperately need to get this into third-party applications as soon as possible. It would save me so much time and effort in WhatsApp chats that I’m sort of frustrated it isn’t system-wide yet.

Now that I’ve been using Rambler for an extended period, I’ve made a U-turn on its inclusion, and I’m trusting it more to take notes, send long messages, and dare I say it, compose a few important emails…It’s a sleeper function that I’m enjoying greatly as a lazy typer. I even drafted a few paragraphs of this extended review using Rambler. Add in live transcripts, and it’ll become a “must have” for the lazy among us.

I completely forgot that Pause Point was already on Pixel 11. I’ve tried it a few times, and I don’t know why it isn’t being touted as a bigger deal. It’s one of the few Digital Wellbeing tools that feels like it could curb your phone usage. The rest of the AI stack? It all still feels a little filler. I’m still using Pixel Screenshots on an almost daily basis, but I’m still not finding ways to use many of the major functions that Google keeps touting because of the aforementioned first-party app requirements.

I mentioned modem issues in my initial review; these were temporary. Fully resolved, there is no doubt in my mind that the modem handles signal way better than the Pixel 9 and 10, and VPN connection woes are gone with the last couple of OTA updates, too.

Finally, a quality camera…again

I’m so glad that Google paid attention to some of the major complaints with the Pixel 10 and put in a “proper” big main sensor rather than short-changing buyers with an A-series sensor. The quality jump just gives me confidence that you’re properly equipped for every eventuality.

Next year, I’m fully hoping for some improved ultrawide and telephoto hardware.

To the surprise of nobody, Camera Looks is my outright most used function across every facet of the Pixel 11 this year so far. In the back of my mind, with just about any Pixel, having consistency has been both a blessing and a curse. I spoke about this last year when switching away to Zerocam on the Pixel 10 Pro. I wanted less processing done on my behalf, and Camera Looks just answers that with aplomb.

I have completely switched to using the “Shadows” look. It’s my default setting, and like when using Zerocam, I’m being more picky about what photos I’m taking with this phone. My only gripe is that the recipes you can cook up would be great if saved for specific circumstances. Being able to save these as custom looks with unique names would be a godsend and a real timesaver.

If you just want pure consistency, stick with the default settings and enjoy another great camera with better zoom, a quality main sensor; the rest is just more of the same – which is to say very good for this price bracket.

I wish I had more reasons to use Magic Camera, as my colleague Daniel Bader so aptly states, this is the ultimate family camera function. The outputs are great, and getting both video and photo at the same time is perfect, as you preserve the moment no matter what. 

As I say, maybe I need to force myself to use it more often. I’ve barely touched it since my first week of testing, but I’m more at home playing with regular photos and don’t often need snapshots from Magic Camera. There are people who are going to use this practically every day. I am not one of those people.

Loving the longevity

I can’t say I’ve had a problem with a recent Pixel phone, but the 11 is really solid. I’ve been on a few weekend trips already with this phone, and it hasn’t let me down. Side note: I actually like the AI summaries for battery usage. It feels better tailored than just the list of apps. It’s fairly recent, but I like this tweak and hope it improves over time.

There’s only so many times I can complain about the charging speed before you sort of come to terms with it. At least the Qi2 charging speed has increased to 25W, which isn’t a million miles away from the wired charging speed now. Just give us a little more, and I’ll be happier. That said, I started charging overnight again quite recently, so my complaint is a little moot.

For what it’s worth, the Pixel 11 lasts longer than my Pixel 11 Pro, which is solid and dependable. It’s been a long time since a Pixel had a terrible battery lifespan, put it that way.

What’s it like to own the Pixel 11, and is it worth it?

About upgrading: 9to5Google often gives specific product recommendations. Sometimes, we may suggest not upgrading, due to various reasons including, but not limited to: increased device cost, negligible performance gains, or environmental impact. Whether to upgrade is always your call, but our aim is to help you make as informed a decision as possible.

2026 feels like a sobering year for technology. Not only has real progress slowed drastically in the areas outside artificial intelligence, but we’re expected to pay more for the privilege.

There is a good phone underneath the price hikes. One that, yes, hasn’t changed all that much.

Luckily for most people, the Pixel 11 isn’t as compromised as the Pro models. For a long time, I felt that this was where Google did the best work outside of the A-series. A solid base for all the functionality and features a “normie” would and could want from their mobile companion.

Because the Pixel 11 Pro and Pro XL have some cost prohibitive compromizes, there’s a cost incentive to go for the base model once again. I still struggle to fully recommend that anyone buy the Pixel 11, but it’s the most sensible of the bunch.

We’ll revisit the Pixel 11 again in the next few months to determine what has held up and what hasn’t, so if you prefer even longer testing periods, then check back in another 60-ish days for an updated verdict.

title: Chrome now saves scroll position, filled forms when sending tabs between devices
snippet: Google today announced a trio of new study-focused Chrome features, with the most notable being how the browser will now save scroll position when you send tabs between devices. more…
fullText:
Google today announced a trio of new study-focused Chrome features, with the most notable being how the browser will now save scroll position when you send tabs between devices.

When you send a page from mobile to laptop (or vice versa), Chrome will now save the “exact state of your tab when you send it over.” This includes the scroll position and partially filled-in forms: “if you’re halfway through a 50-page paper on behavioral economics, you can send it to your phone and pick up exactly where you left during your commute.”

On desktop, you can do this from the three-dot overflow menu > Cast, Save, and Share > Send to Your Device. The shortcut can also be added to your toolbar from Customize Chrome (on the New Tab Page) > Toolbar. In Chrome for Android, open Chrome’s share menu for the carousel of options.

Gemini in Chrome now lets you ask questions about videos, podcasts, recordings, and other types of media that aren’t on YouTube. Google touts how the side panel can now “identify key takeaways, find specific information, or clarify confusing moments for almost any audio or video file once you’ve played it through.”

	

Meanwhile, Gemini in Chrome can now generate interactive quizzes with the content of your current tab. This can include Google Docs, YouTube videos, research papers, and more. The tool will “highlight core concepts and help you check your understanding.” Quizzes are coming to English in the US and India on desktop and will come to more regions and mobile in the “coming months.”

Google is highlighting other existing tools like vertical or horizontal tabs, Split View, and tab groups. There’s also immersive reading mode and read aloud.

fullText:
Apple’s iPhone Duo may not have reinvented the Android foldable, but it certainly did put a polish on a number of things. Inlcuded in that list is stylus support on the iPhone Duo, something that was more complicated behind-the-scenes than it initially sounded like, and an effort that Samsung should probably take note of.

Rewinding, Samsung’s Galaxy Z Fold series first added stylus support back in 2022 on the Galaxy Z Fold 3. Samsung made a special version of the S Pen stylus for foldables that didn’t require a battery, but also didn’t stow away inside of the foldable. Still, it was fully supported and a welcome tool, especially as the Galaxy Note series was dying off. But with last year’s Galaxy Z Fold 7, Samsung ditched support for the S Pen in order to make the foldable much thinner.

S Pen support on Galaxy Z Fold 4 and Fold 5

But, of course, Samsung is likely rethinking that decision now that Apple has introduced the iPhone Duo with stylus support.

Apple touts that the iPhone Duo will support the USB-C version of the Apple Pencil that’s otherwise made for iPads. It sounds simple enough, but there’s more to the story. Bloomberg reports that Apple originally wanted to make a dedicated version of Apple Pencil for the iPhone Duo, a version that would have been shorter and able to magnetically hold itself on the Duo’s hinge. 

	

That stylus wasn’t announced as, apparently, Apple ran into “technical problems ahead of mass production” a few months before the Duo was announced, leading to the pivot over to iPad versions of the stylus. The report further notes that Apple’s software update to enable this isn’t “as simple as hitting a button” and that it won’t arrive until “fairly late in 2026.” 

Still, that’s more than Samsung is bringing to the table at this point. Both the Galaxy Z Fold 8 and Fold 8 Ultra lack any support for a stylus, despite rumors of Samsung exploring other ways of offering a stylus on its foldables. The reason the traditional S Pen doesn’t work in these thin form factors is that it requires a physical layer in the display assembly and, as such, adds to the thickness and weight – two pillars that Samsung is hyper-focused on improving with each generation. 

Samsung’s Android competition has embraced stylus support, so between that and Apple’s adoption (mostly the latter, obviously), it’s all the more likely Galaxy Z Fold 9 will bring stylus support page in one form or another. Samsung has left the door open, too.

title: Here’s everything new for Apple Calendar in iOS 27
snippet: iOS 27 is packed with new features for Apple Wallet, Messages, Notes, and other system apps—including Calendar. Here’s everything new for Apple’s Calendar app in iOS 27. more…
fullText:
iOS 27 is packed with new features for Apple Wallet, Messages, Notes, and other system apps—including Calendar. Here’s everything new for Apple’s Calendar app in iOS 27.

Natural language input for events and reminders

Calendar adds a feature in iOS 27 that’s been on my wishlist for years: natural language input.

Apple calls this ‘Smart Event Details,’ and it’s powered by Apple Intelligence. Here’s how it’s described:

Type events in your own words. Apple Intelligence fills in the title, time, location, and invitees as you go.

This works for both events and reminders. You can type in natural language when creating or editing an event, and watch the event details automatically fill in based on what you type.

If you prefer the manual approach, you can toggle this off in Settings, but I’ve been very happy to have it.

Design updates

Apple has updated Calendar’s design in iOS 27 in two main places:

Event details view

Event creation and editing

When you tap an event, it now pops up in a card overlay with a fresh design. Event options have been reorganized and given icons to make them visually pop.

And for event creation and editing, iOS 27 has an updated look too. Like with event details, Apple has reorganized the various options and added icons for each category.

Show as Busy/Free option for iCloud calendars

With modern digital calendars, the ability to mark yourself as busy or free related to a given event is a pretty standard feature. But until iOS 27, that option never existed for iCloud calendars.

If you use a Google calendar inside Apple’s app, you’ll see the event option to show yourself as busy or free. But for iCloud calendars, that’s long been missing.

iOS 27 finally remedies the oversight, offering a free/busy option for iCloud events like you would get for events from Google and other third-party calendar providers.

iOS 27 lets you make Home Screen and Today widgets bigger than ever thanks to a new extra-large size. And Calendar supports two extra-large widgets.

You can set up ’List’ and ‘Up Next’ widgets in the extra-large size. Each is great for showing more events and reminders than ever, so if you have a packed calendar, the new widgets could prove useful.

Extra-large widgets take up a lot of screen real estate, but they should prove especially handy on the iPhone Duo’s extra-large display.

Siri AI upgrades

It’s worth mentioning that Siri AI comes with plenty of upgrades relevant to the Calendar app.

Siri gains onscreen awareness, understands your personal context, and is overall more intelligent and capable than ever before. That means it’s a much better tool for managing your calendar. In my use of iOS 27, I’ve found myself relying much more on Siri for handling events and reminders.

There’s also a new visual intelligence button in the event creation screen that lets you scan an event flyer with the new Siri mode in the Camera app. Siri then creates a new event with the details.

title: Rare ‘Antennagate’ press conference Q&A video surfaces online
snippet: The Q&A session of one of Apple’s most notable events in the last 20 years has surfaced online, and you should watch it before it vanishes. Watch it below. more…
fullText:
The Q&A session of one of Apple’s most notable events in the last 20 years has surfaced online, and you should watch it before it vanishes. Watch it below.

Watch it before Apple pulls it

Even if you didn’t follow Apple closely back in 2010, you have probably heard about Antennagate and the last-minute press conference that pulled Steve Jobs from a family vacation in Hawaii.

If you’re just joining us, here’s what happened: Soon after Apple released the iPhone 4, users noticed that the cell signal would drop significantly depending on how they held the device.

The commotion around this was big enough that Apple scheduled an emergency event just weeks after the iPhone 4 hit the shelves.

In it, Jobs explained that the signal drop wasn’t exclusive to the iPhone 4, but that users would have the choice to either get a free case to prevent their hands from making direct contact with the antenna, or return the phone for a full refund.

After the event, Jobs was joined by then-COO Tim Cook and Bob Mansfield, Apple’s senior vice president of Mac Hardware Engineering, for a Q&A with the press.

Since then, there have been multiple accounts of what was said during the Q&A, including John Gruber’s recollections from asking the question that prompted Jobs, Cook, and Mansfield to pull their caseless iPhones out of their pockets, resulting in one of the more memorable photos from that era. However, the actual video of the session had never surfaced. Until now.

	

Earlier this week, YouTube channel Sir Mix-A-Lot Rare Music (no apparent relation to the actual Sir Mix-A-Lot) published the entire 47-minute Q&A session, which you can watch below:

There is no information on how the channel obtained the video or whether Apple plans to file a copyright takedown request. But now that the footage is out there, copies could easily resurface elsewhere even if the original upload disappears.

The mere fact that the video is still up is a good sign. That said, if you want to see this little piece of Apple history for yourself, you might want to watch it sooner rather than later.

Did you already follow Apple back in the Antennagate days? Let us know in the comments.

title: YouTube announces Custom Feeds, GIF comments, and ’Your podcast lineup’
snippet: At Made on YouTube 2026 today, YouTube announced a slew of new features. We’ve highlighted the capabilities that will impact the viewer experience over the coming months. more…
fullText:
At Made on YouTube 2026 today, YouTube announced a slew of new features. We’ve highlighted the capabilities that will impact the viewer experience over the coming months.

YouTube app

Custom Feeds will let you conversationally create a dedicated tab from the Homepage for “specific moods, routines, or your latest interests.” Multiple feeds can be created, with examples including “evening wind down with long documentaries” or “new DIY creators.” This feature is coming to US users on web, mobile, and TVs “soon.”

Ask YouTube is getting shopping features that let you “receive organized video recommendations, such as a comparison table that includes product attributes and categories based on your preferences.”

Once you click on a video that interests you most, you can continue asking more questions about the product directly on the video’s watch page.

This fall, YouTube comments will support GIFs. The mobile comment box will let you search a library of GIFs with this type of commenting available on videos and Shorts.

	

The in-app direct messaging feature is adding support for group chats. This is coming this fall in the US, UK, Singapore, Brazil, and some European countries.

YouTube Music + Podcasts

YouTube Music is getting a “personalized AI-audio guide” called Your podcast lineup. You get a “weekly spoken preview of recommended shows” that will dive into why you’ll like them. It then proceeds to suggested episodes, with this touted as being a “completely eyes-optional and hands-free” experience.

Meanwhile, the Ask Music chat found in the Home tab is getting new features that let you “customize your queue or dive deeper into artist lore.”

Both updates are “coming soon to YouTube Music and Premium subscribers worldwide.”

YouTube will stream Coachella through 2030. The 2027 edition will mark “15 years of bringing the desert festival experience to fans worldwide.”

YouTube Shorts 

	

YouTube is introducing a Shorts series feature that lets Creators organize their Shorts into seasons and episodes for a more structured and episodic experience. This is rolling out starting today. 

In a related development, the Shorts feed will start to recommend posts. Google shared that over 300 million users engage with Posts on YouTube every day. These text posts will also be coming to TVs in the “coming months.”

For YouTube Creators 

YouTube is piloting a Live auto-dubbing feature in early 2027 that “automatically translates your speech in real time” to let viewers “listen along in their preferred language as you speak.”

YouTube is testing “opt-in AI-powered comment moderation.” It will learn your “unique moderation style and needs over time.”
